This contrasts with the vanilla U-Net, which uses two standard convolutions per operation. Experimental results demonstrate that SDU-Net surpasses vanilla U-Net, Attention U-Net (AttU-Net), and Recurrent Residual U-Net (R2U-Net) across all four tested segmentation tasks. Furthermore, SDU-Net achieves this superior performance with significantly fewer parameters, using approximately 40% of vanilla U-Net's, 17% of AttU-Net's, and 15% of R2U-Net's parameter count.

Distributed Gradient Descent (DGD) offers an efficient approach to implementing Gradient Descent (GD), particularly for large datasets. This efficiency stems from dividing computational tasks into smaller subtasks, which are then distributed among various computing servers (CSs) for parallel execution. In typical parallel processing, the per-iteration waiting time is bottlenecked by the slowest server. To address this, recent advancements include coded DGD techniques, which mitigate the impact of straggling servers by assigning redundant computational tasks to CSs.

Most current DGD schemes, whether employing coded computation or coded communication, involve non-straggling CSs transmitting a single message per iteration once their assigned tasks are complete. However, even straggling servers often manage to complete a portion of their tasks, despite not finishing all of them. This paper proposes a novel approach: allowing each CS to transmit multiple messages per iteration. This ensures that the maximum possible number of completed computations, including those from straggling servers, are reported to the aggregating server (AS). Our numerical results demonstrate that this strategy significantly reduces the average completion time per iteration, with only a marginal increase in per-server communication load.

Object recognition and keypoint estimation, widely adopted recognition tasks, predominantly rely on computationally and memory-intensive deep networks. This poses significant challenges for deployment on low-power embedded devices, highlighting the critical need for models with reduced storage and computational demands. The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) offers a potential solution, positing that dense neural networks harbor smaller, high-performing subnetworks.

This work presents the first empirical investigation of LTH for model pruning in object detection, instance segmentation, and keypoint estimation. Our findings indicate that lottery tickets derived from ImageNet pretraining do not readily transfer to these downstream tasks. We provide a methodology for identifying effective lottery tickets, achieving up to 80% overall sparsity across various sub-tasks without performance degradation. Furthermore, we analyze the performance characteristics of these "trained tickets" in relation to task attributes such as object size, frequency, and detection difficulty.

We quantify, using $L^2$ function space, the difference between a finite-width network trained on limited samples and the idealized kernel dynamics of infinite width and data. Our bounds reveal that the network preferentially learns the Neural Tangent Kernel's leading eigenfunctions across the entire input space, not just the training set. This bias is solely determined by the model architecture and input distribution, independent of the target function, even if it falls outside the kernel's RKHS. This finding applies to deep architectures, including fully connected, convolutional, and residual layers. Notably, high-probability bounds can be achieved up to a stopping time without requiring polynomial growth in width relative to sample size. Our proof leverages the low effective rank of the Fisher Information Matrix at initialization, indicating a model's effective dimension significantly smaller than its parameter count. We believe the theoretical implications of local capacity control, as evidenced by the low effective rank of the Fisher Information Matrix, warrant further investigation.

The global proliferation of novel coronavirus pneumonia presents an unparalleled strain on healthcare systems and disease control strategies. COVID-19 not only severely impairs respiratory function, leading to life-threatening complications, but also afflicts vital organs such as the heart, kidneys, and brain, potentially resulting in long-term sequelae. Current COVID-19 detection relies on reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). However, many nations grappling with epidemic peaks face severe limitations in medical resources, precluding widespread genetic sequencing and delaying crucial isolation and treatment for numerous patients.

In response to this challenge, our research investigates the analytical and diagnostic potential of deep learning applied to chest radiographs. We introduce Cascade-SEMEnet, an architecture comprising cascaded SEME-ResNet50 and SEME-DenseNet169 networks. Both components of Cascade-SEMEnet utilize large input sizes, incorporate SE-Structure, and employ MoEx and histogram equalization for data augmentation. Initially, SEME-ResNet50 screens chest X-rays to classify them as normal, bacterial pneumonia, or viral pneumonia. Subsequently, SEME-DenseNet169 performs fine-grained classification of viral pneumonia, specifically identifying cases attributable to COVID-19.

Our work introduces a novel approach for autonomously discovering the underlying differential equations within a dataset, a key objective of model discovery. While Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have shown significant potential in this area, the development of a fully-differentiable model capable of explicitly learning these equations has remained a challenge. We address this by integrating neural network surrogates with Sparse Bayesian Learning (SBL), resulting in a robust model discovery algorithm that we demonstrate across diverse datasets.

Furthermore, we identify a link between our method and multitask learning, which we leverage to develop the Physics-Informed Normalizing Flow (PINF). We present a proof-of-concept for the PINF, demonstrating its ability to directly learn a density model from single-particle data. This research expands the applicability of PINNs to a broader range of neural network architectures and establishes a connection between neural network-based surrogates and the well-developed field of Bayesian parameter inference.

**Objective:** This study explores the application of deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for automated measurements of fetal body parts—specifically head circumference, biparietal diameter, abdominal circumference, and femur length—from fetal ultrasound videos. The ultimate goal is to estimate gestational age and fetal weight.

**Approach:** We developed FUVAI, a novel multi-task CNN-based algorithm designed for spatio-temporal fetal ultrasound feature extraction and standard plane detection. We assessed FUVAI's performance on 50 freehand fetal ultrasound video scans, comparing its biometric measurements against those obtained by five experienced sonographers who performed measurements at two separate time points, at least two weeks apart. We also quantified both intra- and inter-observer variability.

**Main Results:** FUVAI's automated fetal biometric measurements were found to be comparable to those performed by experienced sonographers. The discrepancies observed were within the established range of inter- and intra-observer variability. Furthermore, statistical analysis confirmed that these differences were not significant when comparing FUVAI's measurements to those of any individual medical expert.

**Significance:** We propose that FUVAI holds promise for assisting sonographers in clinical settings by providing automated measurements and suggesting optimal measuring frames. Importantly, FUVAI can accomplish these tasks rapidly.

Federated Learning enables model training on decentralized data, preserving privacy by eliminating the need for central data aggregation. A significant challenge to its widespread adoption is effectively managing data heterogeneity (non-IID distribution). This paper introduces a novel Divide-and-Conquer training approach designed to enhance the performance of the widely used FedAvg algorithm in non-IID environments, overcoming its known limitations. Our method employs a new Cosine-distance based Weight Divergence metric to identify the optimal division point within a Deep Learning network, separating it into class-agnostic initial layers and class-specific deeper layers for the Divide and Conquer strategy. We demonstrate that this methodology achieves comparable, and sometimes superior, model accuracy to state-of-the-art aggregation algorithms such as FedProx and FedMA. Furthermore, we show that our approach offers computational and bandwidth efficiencies under specific conditions.

Gradient Boosting Decision Trees (GBDTs) are widely used machine learning algorithms, with implementations available in libraries like LightGBM and Scikit-Learn. Current implementations typically build trees offline using a greedy approach. This work investigates methods to transform existing GBDT implementations into neural network architectures while preserving performance. This conversion aims to enable online updates of decision splits and allow for the modification of split points through neural architecture search. We also derive learning bounds for our proposed neural network model.

Deep neural networks (DNNs), while prominent in machine learning, are black-box models that lack explainability for their predictions. Neural additive models (NAMs) have recently emerged to address this, offering interpretability without sacrificing predictive accuracy. This paper introduces a novel NAM approach specifically designed for multivariate nowcasting (NC) problems, a critical area in machine learning.

For multivariate time-series data typical in NC, explaining predictions necessitates understanding the contribution of each input value to the variables at distinct time steps. Our proposed NAM-NC, built upon generalized additive models, successfully quantifies the importance of individual input values across multiple variables and time steps.

Through experiments on a toy example and two real-world datasets, we demonstrate that NAM-NC achieves prediction accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art neural networks for multivariate time-series data, while crucially providing explainable importance scores for each input. Furthermore, we explore complexity reduction in NAM-NC through parameter-sharing networks, showing that its hard-tied feature network extracts effective explanations even with reduced complexity.

Our novel method identifies anomalies in time series, a crucial capability across diverse fields such as autonomous vehicles, finance, marketing, medical diagnostics, and epidemiology. Built upon self-supervised deep learning, our approach addresses a key challenge: unlike image-based anomaly detection, time series data lacks readily available powerful transformations. To overcome this, we introduce Local Neural Transformations (LNT), a method that learns local time series transformations directly from data. LNT assigns an anomaly score to each time step, enabling anomaly detection within the series. We theoretically demonstrate that our unique training objective surpasses prior deep anomaly detection methods in suitability for transformation learning. Experimental results show LNT's effectiveness in detecting anomalies within speech segments from the LibriSpeech dataset and outperforming previous work in identifying cyber-physical system interruptions. Furthermore, visualizations of the learned transformations offer valuable insights into their characteristics.

Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) like traffic monitoring require real-time data on vehicle types (cars, trucks, buses) from critical roads. Traditional methods, relying on GPS or camera networks, are either privacy-invasive or costly. This paper introduces SenseMag, a low-cost, non-invasive method using a pair of magnetic sensors on straight road sections to recognize vehicle types. SenseMag filters noise and segments magnetic signals precisely when vehicles arrive at or depart from each sensor. It then employs a hierarchical model to estimate vehicle speed, which in turn determines vehicle length using predicted speed, sampling cycles, and sensor node distance. Finally, SenseMag classifies vehicle types by analyzing vehicle length and extracting temporal/spectral features from the magnetic signals. The design of filters, features, and hyperparameters incorporates semi-automated learning. Extensive real-world field tests in Shenzhen, China, demonstrate SenseMag's superior performance compared to existing methods.

Training deep learning models on extensive datasets demands significant time and resources. This challenge motivates the creation of compact, synthetic datasets capable of sufficiently training these models. Recent research has explored condensing image datasets using complex bi-level optimization. For example, dataset condensation (DC) aligns network gradients from large real datasets with those from small synthetic datasets, optimizing network weights over multiple steps in each outer iteration.

However, current methods have limitations: they are not directly applicable to discrete graph data, and their nested optimization makes the condensation process computationally intensive. To address this, we propose an efficient dataset condensation method specifically for graph datasets. We model the discrete graph structure probabilistically and introduce a one-step gradient matching scheme that bypasses network weight training. Our theoretical analysis indicates that this approach generates synthetic graphs leading to reduced classification loss on real graphs. Extensive experiments across various graph datasets confirm the effectiveness and efficiency of our method, enabling significant dataset size reduction.

Despite growing interest in fine-grained recognition within our field, a precise definition for "fine-grained" has remained elusive. This work introduces a framework, rooted in clustering theory, for quantifying dataset granularity. We posit that granularity is determined not only by data samples and their labels, but also by the chosen distance function. We propose an axiomatic framework outlining essential properties for a dataset granularity measure, offering examples that fulfill these criteria. Through experiments on hierarchically labeled datasets of varying granularity, we evaluate each measure. Our findings reveal that several commonly used datasets, widely considered fine-grained, actually contain substantial subsets that are significantly more coarse-grained than datasets typically categorized as coarse-grained. Furthermore, our investigation into the relationship between dataset granularity and various factors indicates that fine-grained datasets present greater challenges in learning, transfer learning, and few-shot learning, while also exhibiting increased vulnerability to adversarial attacks.

This paper investigates the approximation capabilities of ReLU neural networks with norm-constrained weights. We establish upper and lower bounds on the approximation error for smooth function classes. The lower bound, derived using the Rademacher complexity of neural networks, may have broader implications. We then apply these approximation bounds to analyze the convergence of regression with norm-constrained neural networks and distribution estimation via GANs, specifically demonstrating convergence rates for over-parameterized neural networks. Furthermore, we show that GANs can achieve optimal learning rates for probability distributions when the discriminator is an appropriately chosen norm-constrained neural network.

Feature Learning automatically extracts relevant information from data. This field underpins the current deep learning trend, a set of empirically successful methods. However, a theoretical understanding of various feature learning schemes is still needed. This work introduces a theoretical framework for feature learning, defining conditions under which features can be learned without supervision. We also propose using rate-distortion theory and its extensions to assess feature quality.

Deep learning models (DLMs) excel in speech recognition, yet training them, especially large-scale production models, can be time-consuming. While various parallel training algorithms exist to boost efficiency, choosing the best one for a specific task remains challenging due to insufficient comparative analysis. This paper addresses this gap by systematically evaluating four prominent parallel training algorithms—asynchronous stochastic gradient descent (ASGD), blockwise model-update filtering (BMUF), bulk synchronous parallel (BSP), and elastic averaging stochastic gradient descent (EASGD)—for speech recognition. Using feed-forward deep neural networks (DNNs) and convolutional, long short-term memory, DNNs (CLDNNs) on the 1000-hour LibriSpeech corpus, our experiments reveal BMUF as the superior choice for acoustic model training. It consistently demonstrates stability, excellent scalability with GPUs, reproducibility, and often surpasses single-GPU SGD performance. ASGD may serve as an alternative in certain scenarios.

Optimization techniques are frequently employed early in the design process to explore a wide range of potential solutions. For this purpose, illumination algorithms like MAP-Elites offer a compelling alternative to traditional optimization methods. Unlike classic algorithms that typically yield a single near-optimal solution, illumination algorithms generate diverse, high-quality solutions in a single execution. However, their current need for extensive function evaluations limits their practical application.

This paper introduces Surrogate-Assisted Illumination (SAIL), a novel illumination algorithm designed to address this limitation. SAIL utilizes surrogate modeling to map the design space based on user-defined features, significantly reducing the number of fitness evaluations required. We demonstrate SAIL's efficiency on a 2-dimensional airfoil optimization problem, where it generates hundreds of diverse, high-performing designs with orders of magnitude fewer evaluations than MAP-Elites or CMA-ES. Furthermore, SAIL proves capable of mapping high-performing designs in realistic 3-dimensional aerodynamic tasks using accurate flow simulation. By enabling data-efficient design exploration, SAIL empowers designers to understand the full spectrum of possibilities, moving beyond simple objective-based optimization to consider a broader range of high-performing designs.

Network data is becoming an increasingly valuable resource for quantitative, data-driven public policy research. These datasets often possess a high degree of complexity, characterized by intricate correlations and interdependencies. While this richness offers significant potential for policy insights, it also presents a challenge: effectively extracting meaningful information. This challenge necessitates the development of novel data analysis methodologies.

This report outlines a research agenda focused on critical methodological problems, the resolution of which would significantly advance various areas of policy research. We then explore recent breakthroughs in applying deep learning to network data, demonstrating how these methods can address many of the identified methodological challenges. We specifically highlight deep generative methods, which can create realistic synthetic networks. These synthetic networks are particularly useful for microsimulation and agent-based models, providing valuable insights for key public policy questions.

Building upon these advancements, we introduce a new generative framework designed for large social contact networks, commonly employed in epidemiological modeling. For comparative understanding, we also contrast these neural network-based approaches with traditional Exponential Random Graph Models. Finally, we discuss remaining open problems that require further investigation.

Deep learning's growing role in predicting and controlling physical systems highlights the critical need for accurate representations. These representations must align with physical laws. For discrete data, this alignment can be achieved by incorporating informed priors during learning, though not all discretization priors maintain essential physical structures.

This paper introduces Symplectic Momentum Neural Networks (SyMo), models derived from a discrete mechanics formulation for non-separable systems. This approach constrains SyMo models to preserve crucial geometric properties, like momentum and a symplectic form, enabling effective learning from limited datasets. Additionally, SyMo can learn dynamics solely from pose data.

We further enhance SyMo by integrating variational integrators through an implicit root-finding layer, resulting in End-to-End Symplectic Momentum Neural Networks (E2E-SyMo). Experiments with pendulums and cartpoles demonstrate that this framework not only facilitates learning from limited data but also ensures the preservation of the symplectic form, leading to superior long-term performance.

We present novel depth-based separation results for feed-forward neural networks. Our findings demonstrate that deeper networks more effectively approximate a range of simple and natural functions compared to shallower ones, even when the latter are significantly larger. This includes indicators of balls and ellipses, non-linear functions radial with respect to the $L_1$ norm, and smooth non-linear functions. We further validate these theoretical insights experimentally: increased depth, rather than increased width, proves more beneficial for learning an indicator of a unit ball.

Neural networks, particularly deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs), excel at medical image segmentation, achieving impressive results rapidly when leveraging GPU acceleration. However, alternatives exist for scenarios where GPUs are unavailable. This study investigates the performance of two random forest approaches against a state-of-the-art deep CNN for medical image segmentation. Using the PhC-C2DH-U373 and retinal imaging datasets for comparison, we found that while the deep CNN delivered the best overall performance, one of the random forest methods achieved a comparably high level of accuracy. This suggests that random forest approaches can serve as a viable alternative to deep CNNs, enabling effective medical image segmentation without the need for GPU hardware.

Microarray technology enables the simultaneous monitoring of thousands of genes under various experimental conditions. This technique is instrumental in identifying co-expressed genes within specific cells or tissues that are actively involved in protein synthesis. Analyzing gene expression through this method is a crucial task in bioinformatics research. Cluster analysis of gene expression data has proven particularly useful for identifying co-expressed genes and forming biologically relevant groupings of both genes and samples.

This paper analyzes K-Means with Automatic Generation of Merge Factor for ISODATA (AGMFI) to cluster microarray datasets based on the ISODATA algorithm. AGMFI distinguishes itself by automatically generating initial values for merge and split factors, as well as maximum merge times, rather than requiring the selection of efficient values as in standard ISODATA. Typically, initial seeds for each cluster are chosen either sequentially or randomly, but the quality of the final clusters can be influenced by these initial selections. Recognizing that the optimal number of clusters is often unpredictable in real-world applications, current research efforts are focused on developing clustering algorithms that do not require a predefined initial number of clusters.

This paper introduces MarsExplorer, an OpenAI Gym-compatible environment designed to apply Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) to the challenge of exploring and covering unknown terrains. MarsExplorer reframes this robotics problem for DRL applications, allowing various off-the-shelf algorithms to be used. Policies developed within MarsExplorer can be directly implemented on robotic platforms, bypassing the need for complex simulation models or additional learning phases for adaptation. A key feature is its controllable, multi-dimensional procedural terrain generation, which is crucial for fostering policies with robust generalization.

We train and evaluate four state-of-the-art DRL algorithms (A3C, PPO, Rainbow, and SAC) within MarsExplorer, comparing their performance against average human-level benchmarks. Further experimental analysis investigates how MarsExplorer's multi-dimensional difficulty setting impacts the learning capabilities of PPO, identified as the top-performing algorithm. Notably, a significant achievement is the generation of an exploration policy that spontaneously follows a Hilbert curve, without explicit instruction or direct/indirect reward for such trajectories. The paper concludes with an evaluation of the PPO-learned policy.

Designing the best controllers for dynamic systems often means solving optimization problems under strict real-time deadlines. These deadlines dictate which numerical methods are suitable: highly accurate but slow routines are swapped for faster, less precise ones, sacrificing accuracy for speed. This paper introduces methods to enhance the quality of these optimized control policies within a given computational limit. We accomplish this through a "hypersolvers" approach, combining a differential equation solver with a neural network. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated in direct and receding-horizon optimal control problems across low and high dimensions, consistently showing improved solution accuracy and control performance.

Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) is a robust method for identifying shared underlying sources across two or more datasets, offering benefits in dimensionality reduction, clustering, classification, feature selection, and data fusion. However, standard CCA overlooks the geometric properties of these common sources.

This paper introduces a novel graph-regularized CCA (gCCA) that incorporates this geometric information, encoded as a graph, through a graph regularizer. This gCCA leverages graph-induced knowledge of common sources while minimizing the distance between canonical variables.

Furthermore, a dual formulation of gCCA is developed for scenarios where the number of data points is less than the data vector dimensions. This dual approach naturally extends to incorporate kernels, leading to graph-kernel CCA (gkCCA) for handling nonlinear data dependencies.

The efficacy of these new linear, dual, and kernel approaches is demonstrated through image classification tests on various real-world datasets, showcasing their advantages over existing methods.

Sparse subspace clustering methods leveraging $\ell^0$-norm sparsity, such as $\ell^0$-Sparse Subspace Clustering ($\ell^0$-SSC)~\citep{YangFJYH16-L0SSC-ijcv}, surpass their $\ell^1$ counterparts like Sparse Subspace Clustering (SSC)~\citep{ElhamifarV13} in effectiveness. However, theoretical understanding of $\ell^0$-SSC has been limited to noise-free data perfectly aligned with subspaces. Real-world data, conversely, are typically noisy and only approximate subspace structures. This paper demonstrates that an optimal solution to the noisy $\ell^0$-SSC optimization problem achieves the crucial subspace detection property (SDP)—the ability to separate data from distinct subspaces—under both deterministic and semi-random models. Our findings offer the first theoretical assurance of noisy $\ell^0$-SSC's correctness concerning SDP on noisy data, highlighting its advantage through significantly less stringent conditions on subspace affinity. To enhance the efficiency of noisy $\ell^0$-SSC, we introduce Noisy-DR-$\ell^0$-SSC, a method proven to recover subspaces from dimensionality-reduced data. This approach initially projects data into a lower-dimensional space via random projection, then applies noisy $\ell^0$-SSC to the reduced data. Experimental results confirm the efficacy of Noisy-DR-$\ell^0$-SSC.

This paper introduces a method for jointly analyzing multiple functionally related structures in classification tasks. Specifically, our approach is motivated by the observation that functionally correlated brain structures exhibit co-variation between individuals with autism and control groups. To address this, we developed a novel method that combines: (1) non-Euclidean statistics, enabling accurate representation of non-Euclidean data within Euclidean spaces, and (2) a non-parametric integrative analysis method capable of decomposing multi-block Euclidean data into joint, individual, and residual components. We demonstrate that the resulting joint structure effectively, robustly, and interpretably identifies underlying patterns of joint variation in multi-block non-Euclidean data. We validated our method by classifying structural shape data collected from individuals who developed Autistic Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and those who did not.

Cybersecurity has emerged as a paramount concern with the widespread adoption of smart applications, particularly in smart homes where numerous IoT devices are deployed. Ensuring secure and trusted mechanisms in such environments is essential for user peace of mind. While accurate detection of cyberattacks is vital, precisely identifying the attack type is crucial for developing effective countermeasures.

Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) have shown significant promise in detecting security attacks within smart applications. However, the inherent complexity of ANN models often hinders user trust in ANN-based security solutions. Furthermore, the selection of appropriate hyperparameters for ANN architecture is critical for accurate detection, especially when differentiating between subcategories of attacks.

This paper proposes a novel model that addresses both the explainability of ANN models and the challenge of hyperparameter selection. Our goal is to create a solution that is easily trusted and readily adopted by smart home users. Additionally, our approach optimizes the hyperparameter selection process by utilizing a subset of the dataset, thereby reducing the overhead associated with ANN architecture design. This distinctive approach...

Semi-supervised learning (SSL) effectively boosts model performance by utilizing unlabeled data. This paper introduces FixMatch, a simple yet powerful combination of two common SSL techniques: consistency regularization and pseudo-labeling. FixMatch generates pseudo-labels from weakly-augmented unlabeled images, retaining only high-confidence predictions. The model is then trained to predict these pseudo-labels when presented with strongly-augmented versions of the same images.

Despite its simplicity, FixMatch achieves state-of-the-art results across various SSL benchmarks, including 94.93% accuracy on CIFAR-10 with 250 labels and 88.61% accuracy with only 40 labels (4 per class). Given FixMatch's resemblance to less effective SSL methods, we conducted a comprehensive ablation study to identify the key factors contributing to its success. Our code is available at https://github.com/google-research/fixmatch.

The functioning of biological and artificial networks presents a significant and ongoing challenge. To uncover underlying principles, researchers are increasingly examining extensive collections of networks, either trained for or naturally adapted to, similar tasks. There is a growing need for standardized analytical tools to determine how network characteristics—like architecture, brain region, or organism—influence neural representations (activations in hidden layers). This paper establishes a robust framework for such analyses by defining a diverse set of metric spaces to quantify representational dissimilarity. Within this framework, we adapt existing representational similarity measures based on canonical correlation analysis to ensure they adhere to the triangle inequality. We also introduce a new metric specifically designed for convolutional layers, accounting for their inherent biases. Furthermore, we develop approximate Euclidean embeddings, allowing network representations to be seamlessly integrated into a wide range of standard machine learning techniques. We validate these methods using large-scale biological datasets (Allen Institute Brain Observatory) and deep learning benchmarks (NAS-Bench-101). Our work reveals connections between neural representations that can be interpreted through anatomical features and model performance.

This paper introduces a new, effective purification-based adversarial defense method designed to counter pre-processor blind white-box and black-box attacks. Our approach is computationally efficient and relies solely on self-supervised learning with general images, eliminating the need for adversarial training or retraining of the classification model.

We begin by empirically demonstrating that adversarial noise—defined as the residual between an original image and its adversarial counterpart—exhibits a near-zero mean and a symmetric distribution. Leveraging this insight, we developed a straightforward iterative Gaussian Smoothing (GS) technique that effectively smooths out adversarial noise, leading to significantly improved robust accuracy. To further enhance this, we propose Neural Contextual Iterative Smoothing (NCIS). NCIS involves training a blind-spot network (BSN) in a self-supervised manner to reconstruct the discriminative features of the original image that might be lost during GS.

Extensive experiments on the large-scale ImageNet dataset, using four different classification models, show that our method achieves competitive standard accuracy and state-of-the-art robust accuracy against even the strongest purifier-blind white-box and black-box attacks. Additionally, we introduce a novel benchmark for evaluating purification methods, utilizing commercial image classification APIs such as AWS, Azure, Clarifai, and Google. We generate adversarial examples through ensemble transfer-based methods.

Correspondence-based shape models are essential for medical imaging applications that statistically analyze anatomies. These models must consistently represent anatomical features across a population to provide accurate shape statistics. Historically, correspondence was established using nearest-neighbor searches for simpler anatomies. More recently, coordinate transformations have been employed to handle increasing anatomical complexity. However, due to complex geometry and population-level variations, coordinate-wise correspondence often fails to reflect true anatomical correspondence. Group-wise approaches offer an alternative by balancing geometric description with statistical compactness but struggle with nonlinear shape correspondence. Recent efforts have leveraged application-specific correspondence by mapping positional data to higher-dimensional feature spaces, though this often requires extensive manual expert input for defining domain-specific features and landmarks. This paper introduces an automated feature learning method using deep convolutional neural networks to extract correspondence-friendly features from shape ensembles. Additionally, an unsupervised domain adaptation scheme augments pre-trained geometric features with new anatomies. We demonstrate our method's effectiveness on anatomical datasets of the human scapula, femur, and pelvis.

Learning regression functions from censored or interval-valued output data is crucial in fields like genomics and medicine. The aim is to predict a real-valued function, even when training labels are presented as intervals. While most current algorithms for this task are linear, this paper explores the use of nonlinear tree models. We propose a margin-based discriminative objective function to learn such trees and present a dynamic programming algorithm that computes the optimal solution in log-linear time. Our empirical results demonstrate that this algorithm achieves state-of-the-art speed and prediction accuracy across several benchmark datasets.

Automatic Speech Scoring (ASS) involves using computers to assess a speaker's language proficiency. ASS systems grapple with complexities like unconstrained grammar, diverse pronunciations, and unstructured speech. While recent deep learning methods have shown potential, most rely on single-audio feature extraction, neglecting crucial speaker-specific context.

To address this, we introduce speaker-conditioned hierarchical modeling, a novel deep learning approach for non-native ASS. Our method leverages the multi-response nature of oral proficiency tests. We extract context vectors from a candidate's various responses and integrate them into our network as speaker-specific context when scoring individual responses.

Compared to strong baselines, our technique significantly improves average model performance by 6.92% (ranging from 4.51% to 12.86%). We provide both quantitative and qualitative evidence highlighting the vital role of this additional context in enhancing ASS.

Our paper introduces a layer-by-layer algorithm for training deep convolutional networks. Each step involves updating a two-layer network using gradient methods, followed by a straightforward clustering process. This approach is inspired by a deep generative model that constructs images progressively, where lower-resolution images represent latent semantic categories.

We analyze the algorithm's convergence rate, assuming the data aligns with this generative model and other specific conditions. While acknowledging that these assumptions may not perfectly reflect natural image generation, we contend that they capture essential characteristics of real-world data.

Empirical results demonstrate our algorithm's practical efficacy on the CIFAR dataset, where it achieves performance comparable to standard convolutional neural networks trained with stochastic gradient descent. Additionally, the proof techniques developed herein may hold broader theoretical significance.

Determining the solubility of hydrocarbon components in natural gas is crucial for operations in petroleum and chemical engineering. This study introduces a novel tool for estimating the solubility of hydrocarbon gases (methane, ethane, propane, and butane) in aqueous electrolyte solutions, utilizing an extreme learning machine (ELM) algorithm. When validated against a comprehensive real-world dataset of 1175 solubility points, the ELM model achieved R-squared values of 0.985 for training and 0.987 for testing, demonstrating high accuracy. Visual comparisons further confirmed the model's predictive capability. Additionally, a sensitivity analysis was performed on the model's input variables to understand their influence on hydrocarbon solubility. This robust and reliable study provides engineers and scientists with a valuable method for determining essential thermodynamic properties, vital for optimizing and designing industrial units like refineries and petrochemical plants.

Active learning, by its nature, generates data with distinct characteristics compared to passively sampled data. This fundamental difference suggests the potential for employing unique inference procedures in active learning that deviate from those traditionally used in passive learning. We explore this concept through the specific application of active learning with cost-weighted Support Vector Machines (SVMs) for imbalanced datasets, a common challenge in Human Language Technology (HLT). Our proposed method, InitPA, addresses data imbalance by deriving cost models in active learning from an estimated overall corpus imbalance, calculated from a small, unbiased sample. This approach contrasts with the prevailing passive learning method, which typically bases cost models on the observed imbalance within the labeled training data itself.

Weight-sharing and predictor-based methods are prominent approaches for accelerating neural architecture search. This paper introduces a unified framework that synergistically combines these two techniques. We begin by constructing a SuperNet using a weight-sharing strategy, from which we probabilistically sample individual architectures. To enhance the accuracy of architecture evaluation, we employ a multi-faceted approach: alongside direct evaluation using inherited weights, we incorporate a few-shot predictor to provide an additional assessment. The final evaluation is a composite score, integrating direct evaluation, the predictor's output, and the architecture's computational cost. This comprehensive evaluation serves as a reward signal for a self-critical policy gradient method used to update architecture probabilities. Furthermore, to mitigate the inherent limitations of conventional weight sharing, we propose a weakly weight-sharing mechanism facilitated by an auxiliary HyperNet. Our WPNAS method demonstrates state-of-the-art performance across diverse datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, within the NATS-Bench, DARTS, and MobileNet search spaces.

We introduce a feed-forward inference method for both belief and neural networks. For belief networks, this method approximates a factorized posterior of all hidden units based on the given input. For neural networks, it propagates input uncertainty through every layer. When noise is injected into neural networks, our method analytically accounts for the resulting uncertainties. This analytical feed-forward propagation is differentiable with respect to parameters, allowing for end-to-end training. Unlike standard neural networks, which typically propagate only means, our approach propagates both mean and variance. This method offers utility in diverse scenarios requiring knowledge of neuron statistics, such as handling uncertain inputs, interpreting sigmoid activations as Bernoulli unit probabilities, training models with injected noise (e.g., dropout) regularization, or estimating activation statistics across datasets (relevant for normalization techniques). Our experiments demonstrate the method's potential in these applications, as well as its current limitations.

Blackwell introduced the concept of approachability in repeated games with vector payoffs in the 1950s, defining geometric conditions and corresponding strategies. These strategies involved calculating "steering directions" by projecting the current average payoff vector onto a convex target set. More recently, Abernethy, Batlett, and Hazan (2011) developed approachability algorithms that utilize the no-regret properties of Online Linear Programming to determine a sequence of steering directions. Their method initially addresses convex cone target sets and then extends to any convex set through embedding. Here, we propose a more direct formulation using the set's support function and Online Convex Optimization algorithms, yielding a general class of approachability algorithms. We also demonstrate that Blackwell's original algorithm and its convergence are a special case of our framework.

Connected vehicle technology is a constantly advancing field, driven by the growth of the Internet of Things (IoT) and innovations in intelligent transportation. Modern vehicles act as data hubs, generating, receiving, and reacting to vast amounts of information automatically. For assisted driving, connected vehicles offer real-time traffic updates. This capability is poised to enhance drivers' experiences, for instance, by informing decisions based on current parking availability. Our work introduces an online, adaptive method for mapping parking availability. We use an information-seeking active sensing strategy to selectively process incoming data, thereby conserving onboard storage and processing power. Parking availability is then estimated using Gaussian Process Regression. Our algorithm outperforms baseline methods in mapping convergence speed and adaptability, all while requiring minimal computational resources.

This paper presents a new physics-informed deep learning framework for discovering governing partial differential equations (PDEs) from limited, noisy data in nonlinear spatiotemporal systems. Our approach leverages deep neural networks for representation learning, physics embedding, automatic differentiation, and sparse regression to: 1) approximate system variable solutions, 2) compute essential derivatives, and 3) identify key derivative terms and parameters that define PDE structure and expressions. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness and robustness through numerical and experimental validation on various PDE systems, considering data scarcity, noise, and different initial/boundary conditions. This computational framework shows promise for closed-form model discovery in applications where large, accurate datasets are difficult to obtain.

This paper introduces data-driven, one-pass streaming algorithms for estimating the number of triangles and four-cycles, key problems in graph analytics often explored in graph data stream literature. Building on recent work by Hsu (2018) and Jiang (2020), who demonstrated the benefits of machine learning-trained oracles in other data stream problems, we investigate the utility of a "heavy edge" oracle across various graph edge streaming models.

For the adjacency list model, we propose a one-pass triangle counting algorithm that significantly improves upon previous space upper bounds achieved without such an oracle. In the arbitrary order model, we present algorithms for both triangle and four-cycle estimation that require fewer passes while maintaining the same space complexity as prior approaches. We also demonstrate the optimality of several of these bounds.

Our analysis includes evaluating algorithm performance under several noise models, demonstrating resilience even when the oracle provides erroneous predictions. This methodology extends prior work on "classical" streaming algorithms, as multi-pass and random order streaming algorithms can be viewed as special instances of our proposed algorithms, where the first pass or random order serves a similar role to our oracle-informed approach.

Manifold learning techniques are increasingly vital as data proliferates. These algorithms uncover a lower-dimensional representation (embedding) of a dataset's structure, significantly reducing dimensionality while preserving critical information. However, how state-of-the-art manifold learning algorithms achieve this transformation remains unclear. For exploratory data analysis, understanding the relationship between the embedding and the original high-dimensional space is crucial.

Our previous work introduced a transparent and interpretable Genetic Programming method for manifold learning, which evolved explicit mappings. A limitation of this approach was the requirement to pre-define the embedding's dimensionality, hindering its application when little is known about a dataset.

This paper addresses that limitation by substantially extending our prior work. We introduce a multi-objective approach that automatically balances manifold quality against dimensionality. Our proposed method is competitive with various baseline and state-of-the-art manifold learning techniques. Moreover, it yields a spectrum of solutions, offering diverse trade-offs between quality and dimensionality. The resulting models are often simple, efficient, and interpretably leverage only a few features.

Brain-machine interfaces, designed to interpret human intentions from brain signals in real-world settings, face a significant challenge: the distortion of electroencephalography (EEG) signals by artifacts like walking and head movements. These artifacts can generate high-amplitude signals that obscure the desired EEG data, making accurate intention detection in mobile environments difficult.

To address this, we introduce a reconstruction framework based on generative adversarial networks (GANs), specifically designed for event-related potentials (ERPs) recorded during walking. Our approach utilizes a pre-trained convolutional encoder to generate latent variables, which are then used by a generative model—structured as the inverse of the encoder—to reconstruct the ERPs. A discriminative model then classifies these reconstructed ERPs, validating our framework's effectiveness.

Our results show that the reconstructed signals retain critical ERP components, such as N200 and P300, consistent with ERPs recorded during standing. The accuracy of the reconstructed EEG is comparable to that of raw, noisy EEG signals obtained during walking. Notably, the signal-to-noise ratio of the reconstructed EEG significantly improved by a factor of 1.3. Furthermore, the generative model achieved a low loss of 0.6301, indicating high performance during training. Consequently, the reconstructed ERPs demonstrated improved classification performance.

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) excel at modeling data with intricate temporal dependencies, yet their training has historically been hampered by vanishing or exploding gradients. While architectures like LSTMs and GRUs (and their variations) address these issues through gating mechanisms, the precise impact of these gates on the models' dynamics and trainability remains unclear. This paper investigates randomly initialized LSTMs and GRUs as dynamical systems to understand how gating shapes their key dynamical properties. Employing random matrix theory and mean-field theory, we analyze the state-to-state Jacobians of these networks. Our findings indicate that the GRU's update gate and the LSTM's forget gate can foster the accumulation of slow modes within the dynamics. Furthermore, the GRU's update gate can position the system at a point of marginal stability. We also demonstrate that the GRU's reset gate, along with the LSTM's output and input gates, regulate the Jacobian's spectral radius, with the GRU's reset gate additionally influencing landscape complexity.

Transformer models have recently attracted significant attention due to their effectiveness across diverse fields, including language, vision, and reinforcement learning. In natural language processing, for instance, Transformers are now a fundamental component of modern deep learning. A proliferation of "X-former" models—such as Reformer, Linformer, Performer, and Longformer—have emerged, enhancing the original Transformer architecture, often by improving computational and memory efficiency. To assist researchers in navigating this rapid expansion, this paper systematically analyzes a curated selection of recent efficiency-focused "X-former" models, offering a structured and comprehensive overview of current research and models across various domains.

This paper investigates adaptive sensing for Cox point processes, a prevalent model in spatial statistics. We address three key problems: maximizing event capture, locating the peak of the intensity function, and mapping its level sets. Our approach models the intensity function as a sample from a truncated Gaussian process, expressed within a specially constructed positive basis. This basis simplifies the positivity constraint on the intensity function. We detail how a minimally descriptive positive basis can be tailored to the covariance kernel and accommodate non-stationarity, drawing connections to existing positive bases. Our adaptive sensing algorithms leverage Langevin dynamics and are founded on posterior sampling (\textsc{Cox-Thompson}) and top-two posterior sampling (\textsc{Top2}) principles. For the latter, the difference between samples proxies the uncertainty. We illustrate our method with applications in environmental monitoring and crime rate modeling, and compare its performance against traditional Bayesian experimental design.

Recent research has extensively explored manipulating images—both generated and real—using StyleGAN's latent spaces, inspired by its capacity to produce highly realistic images across diverse domains. However, identifying semantically meaningful latent manipulations often necessitates laborious human exploration of numerous variables or a pre-annotated dataset for each desired adjustment.

Our work introduces a text-based interface for StyleGAN image manipulation that bypasses this manual effort by leveraging the power of Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) models.

We first propose an optimization method that employs a CLIP-based loss to modify an input latent vector according to a user's text prompt. Next, we present a latent mapper that deduces a text-guided latent manipulation step for a given input image, facilitating quicker and more stable text-based manipulation. Finally, we detail a method for mapping text prompts to input-agnostic directions within StyleGAN's style space, enabling interactive text-driven image manipulation.

Our extensive results and comparisons confirm the effectiveness of these approaches.

This paper theoretically investigates the expressive power of Spectral Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), a class of GNNs leveraging graph signal filters. While recent advancements have enabled models to learn arbitrary spectral filters, a comprehensive analysis of their expressive capabilities has been lacking.

We demonstrate that even spectral GNNs without nonlinearity can generate arbitrary graph signals, provided two conditions are met: 1) the graph Laplacian has no multiple eigenvalues, and 2) node features contain all frequency components. Furthermore, we establish a link between the expressive power of spectral GNNs and Graph Isomorphism (GI) testing, a common metric for spatial GNNs.

Moving beyond theoretical expressiveness, we explore the empirical performance variations among spectral GNNs with equivalent expressive power, approaching this from an optimization standpoint. This analysis motivates the use of an orthogonal basis where the weight function aligns with the graph signal density in the spectrum.

Inspired by these findings, we propose JacobiConv. This novel model employs a Jacobi basis, capitalizing on its orthogonality and adaptability to various weight functions. Remarkably, JacobiConv achieves superior performance across synthetic and real-world datasets, despite eschewing nonlinearity, outperforming all baseline models.

The linear quadratic regulator (LQR) problem has become a key theoretical model for applying reinforcement learning to control complex dynamical systems with continuous states and actions. Unlike most current research, our work addresses multiplicative noise models. These models are increasingly important because they explicitly account for inherent system uncertainty and variability, leading to improved controller robustness. Robustness is a critical and underexplored challenge in reinforcement learning; methods that neglect uncertainty can yield fragile policies or fail to converge. Moreover, deliberately introducing multiplicative noise into learning algorithms can enhance policy robustness, as seen in domain randomization techniques. While policy gradient algorithms typically involve non-convex optimization, we demonstrate that the multiplicative noise LQR cost exhibits "gradient domination." This property allows us to prove global convergence of policy gradient algorithms to the optimal control policy, with polynomial dependence on problem parameters. Our findings apply to both scenarios where the system model is known and where it is unknown, with policy gradients estimated from sampled system trajectories.

Game theory often models systems of competing agents. When agents are rational, equilibrium concepts like Nash equilibrium predict the most probable outcomes. However, real-world games are frequently influenced by external data—context—that agents cannot control, such as weather impacting traffic or fiscal policy affecting market economies. In many cases, we only observe game equilibria, while the agents' underlying cost functions remain unknown.

This paper presents Nash Fixed Point Networks (N-FPNs), a new type of implicit neural network designed to predict these equilibria solely from their context. N-FPNs combine data-driven modeling with explicit constraints on agent actions. They are compatible with the recent Jacobian-Free Backpropagation technique, which significantly accelerates training compared to previous models. Furthermore, N-FPNs introduce a novel constraint decoupling method that eliminates the need for expensive projections. Numerical examples demonstrate the effectiveness of N-FPNs across various game types, including atomic and non-atomic scenarios like traffic routing.

This paper introduces an unsupervised, data-driven method for predicting real-time locational marginal prices (RTLMPs). Our approach utilizes a novel data structure that organizes diverse, system-wide market data streams into "market data images and videos." This allows us to frame the RTLMP prediction problem as a video prediction task. We then employ a generative adversarial network (GAN)-based video prediction model to capture spatio-temporal correlations in historical RTLMPs and forecast system-wide RTLMPs for the upcoming hour. Prediction accuracy is further enhanced by an autoregressive moving average (ARMA) calibration method. A key advantage of our RTLMP prediction method is its reliance solely on public market data, eliminating the need for confidential information regarding system topology, model parameters, or operational specifics. Case studies using public data from ISO New England (ISO-NE) and Southwest Power Pool (SPP) confirm the method's ability to learn spatio-temporal RTLMP correlations and deliver accurate predictions.

Multi-label learning has garnered significant attention within the machine learning community. A common approach, the Problem Transformation method, converts multi-label problems into familiar single-label ones. Among these, Binary Relevance stands out due to its simplicity and efficiency. However, a key limitation of Binary Relevance is its inability to account for correlations between labels, which can hinder its performance on certain tasks.

This paper introduces a novel multi-label learning algorithm, the Multi-label Parallel Support Vector Machine (MLPSVM), which is also applicable to single-label classification. MLPSVM builds upon standard Support Vector Machines by replacing the traditional single decision hyperplane with two parallel decision hyperplanes. Through experimental comparisons with other multi-label learning algorithms, MLPSVM demonstrates strong performance on various datasets.

Nearest neighbor methods are increasingly used in official statistics, particularly for imputation and statistical matching. They are also fundamental to machine learning, where numerous variations exist. The appropriate distance function is primarily determined by the variable types. However, effectively handling mixed-type variables—a common scenario in official statistics—remains a challenge due to limited options.

The Gower's similarity coefficient, specifically its complement, is the most widely adopted distance measure for mixed-type variables. Its appeal stems from its range (0 to 1) and its ability to accommodate missing values. A drawback of the standard, unweighted Gower's distance is the uneven contribution of individual variables to the overall distance, which arises from their differing natures.

This article proposes modifications to the unweighted Gower's distance to address these limitations. Specifically, it suggests alterations in calculating the distance for interval and ratio-scaled variables. Simple adjustments aim to mitigate the impact of outliers on the scaled Manhattan distance, while other modifications, based on kernel density estimation, seek to balance the contributions of different variable types. The effectiveness of these proposed methods is then evaluated.

Object proposal techniques employing a dense anchoring scheme have been widely used in scene text detection to achieve high recall. While this approach significantly improves accuracy, it incurs substantial computational costs associated with searching, regression, and classification. This paper introduces an anchor selection-based Region Proposal Network (AS-RPN) that extracts text proposals by utilizing a more effective selection of anchors rather than a dense arrangement. Unlike traditional methods, the center, scales, aspect ratios, and orientations of these anchors are learnable, leading to both high recall and a significant reduction in the number of anchors required. When integrated into Faster RCNN, our AS-RPN-based Faster RCNN achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art text detection methods on standard benchmarks (COCO-Text, ICDAR2013, ICDAR2015, and MSRA-TD500) using only single-scale and single-model (ResNet50) testing.

Domain generalization, a field concerned with learning a universal model from multiple source domains, seeks to ensure robust performance on any unobserved but related target domain. This paper addresses domain generalization challenges specifically when domain shifts arise from class-conditional distribution variations across domains. Current methods often falter when these class-conditional distributions exhibit significant variance for a given class. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that extends distributional robust optimization to tackle the class-conditional domain generalization problem. Our method optimizes a classifier's worst-case performance across class-conditional distributions, operating within a Wasserstein ball. This ball is centered at the barycenter of the source conditional distributions. Furthermore, we develop an iterative algorithm to automatically determine the optimal radius for these Wasserstein balls. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed framework significantly outperforms non-domain generalization approaches when applied to unseen target domains.

Finding optimal policies for Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (Dec-POMDPs) is computationally challenging due to information asymmetry, with complexity increasing doubly exponentially with the horizon length. This difficulty is compounded in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), where transition probabilities, observation kernels, and reward functions are unknown. To address this, we propose a general compression framework that utilizes approximate common and private state representations to facilitate the construction of decentralized policies. We quantify the optimality gap when applying dynamic programming (DP) with these approximate states, expressing it in terms of approximation error parameters and remaining time steps. When the compression is exact, our DP approach aligns with existing methods. This framework offers a generalization of several established techniques and provides insights for designing effective deep MARL network architectures within a "centralized learning, distributed execution" paradigm.

The proliferation of deep learning research often hinders the reproducibility and adoption of existing work, largely due to the absence of open-source implementations. Re-implementing these papers in different libraries presents significant challenges. To address this, we introduce DLPaper2Code, an extensible approach that extracts and interprets deep learning design flow diagrams and tables from research papers, converting them into abstract computational graphs. These graphs are then transformed into executable Keras and Caffe code in real-time. We have developed an arXiv-like platform that hosts these automatically generated designs for 5,000 research papers, allowing community rating and editing through an intuitive drag-and-drop interface. Our method was evaluated using a simulated dataset of over 216,000 valid design visualizations, generated via a custom grammar. Experiments demonstrate that our framework achieves over 93% accuracy in extracting content from flow diagrams.

The signature transform, an infinite graded sequence of statistics, characterizes geometric rough paths, including those with bounded variation. While successfully applied in machine learning, particularly in low-dimensional settings, its use in high-dimensional scenarios is hampered by the exponential growth of features in truncated signature transforms. We propose a novel neural network model, inspired by Convolutional Neural Networks, to mitigate this issue. Our model efficiently reduces the number of features in a data-dependent manner. Empirical experiments support its effectiveness.

Machine learning models, by their nature, are imperfect representations of reality. Consequently, learning often occurs despite model misspecification. Here, we introduce a novel analysis of Bayesian Model Averaging's generalization performance under misspecified models and i.i.d. data, employing a new family of second-order PAC-Bayes bounds. Our analysis intuitively demonstrates that Bayesian Model Averaging *underperforms* when models are misspecified. This provides strong theoretical evidence that Bayesian methods are not optimal for predictive learning unless the model class is perfectly specified. Leveraging these new second-order PAC-Bayes bounds, we derive a new class of Bayesian-like algorithms, implementable as variational and ensemble methods. These algorithms yield a new posterior distribution, distinct from the traditional Bayesian posterior, which leads to improved generalization performance in posterior predictive distributions. We validate these findings through experiments with Bayesian neural networks.

Large pre-trained language models have shown promise in generating code from natural language specifications, offering a flexible approach to program synthesis. However, their practical application is often hindered by their tendency to produce syntactically or semantically incorrect code.

This paper introduces **Synchromesh**, a novel framework designed to significantly enhance the reliability of pre-trained models for code generation. Synchromesh operates through two key components:

1.  **Target Similarity Tuning (TST):** This innovative method for semantic example selection retrieves few-shot examples from a training bank. TST learns to identify natural language descriptions that refer to similar target programs, even when their surface-level linguistic features differ.

2.  **Constrained Semantic Decoding (CSD):** Synchromesh feeds the selected examples to a pre-trained language model and then samples programs using CSD. This general framework constrains the model's output to generate only valid programs in the target language. CSD enforces these constraints on partial outputs, enabling the sampling of complete and correct programs without requiring re-training or fine-tuning of the language model.

We evaluated Synchromesh by synthesizing code from natural language descriptions using GPT-3 and Codex across three real-world languages: SQL queries, Vega-Lite visualizations, and SMCalFlow programs. These domains allowed us to demonstrate CSD's ability to enforce a wide range of rich constraints, including syntax, scope, typing rules, and contextual logic. We observe

This paper introduces a dataset of high-resolution images featuring 13 unique micro-PCBs, captured from diverse rotations and perspectives. Each image is meticulously labeled with its PCB type, rotation category, and perspective category. We then detail experiments investigating how different combinations of rotations and perspectives in training data affect test accuracy. Our study also explores the efficacy of data augmentation in simulating unseen rotations and perspectives. All experiments utilize Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), both with and without Homogeneous Vector Capsules (HVCs), to assess the capsules' ability to better encode the equivariance of micro-PCB sub-components. Our findings indicate that the highest classification accuracy on micro-PCB data is achieved by training a neural network equipped with HVCs, capable of modeling sub-component equivariance, and diverse training perspectives.

This paper introduces a differentiable linear quadratic Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework designed for safe imitation learning. The framework guarantees closed-loop stability of the learned controller by incorporating a terminal cost function derived from the discrete-time algebraic Riccati equation (DARE). A key contribution is the analytical derivation of the DARE solution's derivative, which enables the use of differentiation-based learning methods. The paper also highlights the structure of the MPC optimization problem: an augmented Lagrangian method maintains feasibility during training while enforcing strict state and input constraints, and a pre-stabilizing controller ensures the accuracy of MPC solutions and derivatives at each iteration. The framework's learning capabilities are demonstrated through numerical studies.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) are increasingly used in crucial safety-critical applications where reliable predictions are essential. However, despite their powerful predictive abilities, current DNNs lack an inherent way to quantify and propagate the significant input data uncertainty often present in such applications. This uncertainty is frequently epistemic, stemming from various factors like insufficient knowledge of the data generation process, imprecision, ignorance, or a poor understanding of physical phenomena. While recent methods have addressed parameter uncertainty, approaches for end-to-end training of DNNs that account for epistemic input data uncertainty are less common and often problem-specific. Here, we introduce the Deep Interval Neural Network (DINN), a DNN optimized with gradient-based methods that uses interval analysis to quantify both input and parameter uncertainty. Our experiments on an air pollution dataset with sensor uncertainty demonstrate that the DINN can generate accurate, bounded estimates from uncertain input data.

Quick Shift, a widely used mode-seeking and clustering algorithm, is shown to possess finite-sample statistical consistency guarantees for both mode and cluster recovery, given mild distributional assumptions. These findings are then leveraged to develop a consistent modal regression algorithm.

Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), while renowned for their prowess in realistic image synthesis, also demonstrate significant potential in tabular data generation. This paper surveys and critically analyzes recent advancements in tabular GAN applications. We focus on leveraging GANs to generate synthetic data, aiming to narrow the distributional gap between training and test sets. We compare model performance across three scenarios: training on the original dataset, training on the original dataset augmented with GAN-generated data, and training through adversarial sampling of the original data. Our findings indicate that GANs offer a promising solution for mitigating performance degradation caused by disparities in train-test data distributions.

Iconography in art is the study of visual content within artworks, aiming to identify their motifs and themes, as well as the manner in which these are depicted. This field is a dynamic area of research, serving various objectives such as interpreting meaning, tracing the origins and spread of representations across time and space, and examining artistic influences. The growing availability of digital art image archives presents an opportunity to apply Computer Vision techniques to art analysis on an unprecedented scale, offering significant support for iconography research and education.

This paper introduces a new dataset of paintings specifically designed for iconography classification. We present both quantitative and qualitative results from applying a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) classifier to recognize the iconography of artworks. Our proposed classifier demonstrates strong performance in identifying saints in Christian religious paintings, achieving 71.17% Precision, 70.89% Recall, 70.25% F1-Score, and 72.73% Average Precision. This task is particularly challenging due to the visual similarities among different saint representations. Qualitative analysis reveals that the CNN effectively identifies and leverages the traditional iconic motifs that distinguish each saint's portrayal.

Distant supervision (DS) is a powerful technique for expanding datasets to improve relation extraction (RE) models, yet it often introduces significant label noise. Existing approaches, which leverage attention, reinforcement learning, or GANs, are black-box models. Consequently, they lack transparency in sample selection for DS and exhibit instability across various domains. In contrast, this work introduces REIF, a novel model-agnostic instance sampling method for DS that utilizes influence functions (IF). Our method identifies advantageous and disadvantageous instances within a data "bag" using IF, enabling dynamic instance sampling. We develop a fast influence sampling algorithm that dramatically reduces computational complexity from $\mathcal{O}(mn)$ to $\mathcal{O}(1)$ and analyze its robustness with respect to the chosen sampling function. Experimental results demonstrate that REIF, by simply sampling favorable instances during training, outperforms several sophisticated baseline architectures. Furthermore, REIF facilitates interpretable instance selection.

This paper introduces a novel method for structured prediction that embeds complex outputs into a feature space, then solves a regression problem within this space. Unlike traditional approaches where embedding is predefined, our method jointly learns a finite approximation of the output embedding and the regression function. This is achieved by incorporating prior knowledge about outputs and leveraging often-available unsupervised output data. We demonstrate the consistency of our structured predictor and provide an excess risk bound. Furthermore, our approach significantly reduces computational complexity compared to previous output kernel methods. Empirical results across various structured prediction tasks show its versatility and applicability to large datasets.

Traditional neural language models often produce generic, illogical, and unemotional responses. To overcome this, we propose E-SCBA, a syntactically constrained bidirectional-asynchronous approach for emotional conversation generation. Unlike most existing methods that generate replies sequentially, our model asynchronously integrates pre-generated emotion and topic keywords during decoding. Experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly enhances reply diversity, logic, and emotional content compared to baseline models.

Over-parameterized models have garnered significant attention in the age of data science and deep learning. Empirical evidence suggests that these models, such as deep neural networks, despite overfitting training data, can still achieve low test errors and sometimes surpass traditional algorithms designed to prevent overfitting. This work aims to precisely quantify the advantages of data interpolation within the nearest neighbors (NN) algorithm. We examine a class of interpolated weighting schemes and meticulously characterize their asymptotic performance. Our analysis demonstrates a U-shaped performance curve in relation to the degree of data interpolation, proving that a moderate level of interpolation significantly enhances prediction accuracy and statistical stability compared to the optimal kNN algorithm (un-interpolated). This theoretically supports the existence of the second U-shaped curve observed in the recently discovered double descent phenomenon. Our objective is not to advocate for the interpolated-NN method but to gain theoretical understanding of data interpolation, inspired by this phenomenon.

Personalized medicine, an exciting and growing field, aims to tailor medical treatments to individual patient characteristics. A key objective in this paradigm is to identify patient subgroups, defined by their baseline covariates, who would benefit most from a specific treatment compared to alternatives. Current methods for subgroup identification often prioritize enhanced treatment effects but overlook the crucial aspect of subgroup size. However, a truly impactful approach should maximize the number of patients who can benefit from an improved treatment.

This paper introduces an optimal Subgroup Selection Rule (SSR) designed to achieve two goals: maximize the number of selected patients while simultaneously reaching a pre-specified, clinically significant mean outcome (e.g., average treatment effect). We establish two equivalent theoretical formulations of this optimal SSR, leveraging a contrast function that captures the interplay between treatment and covariates in determining the outcome. Furthermore, we propose the ConstrAined PolIcy Tree seArch aLgorithm (CAPITAL) to discover the optimal SSR within an interpretable decision tree framework. This method is versatile, accommodating multiple constraints to discourage the inclusion of patients who might experience negative treatment effects and capable of handling time-to-event data using restricted mean survival time.

Graph representation learning has garnered significant interest due to its broad utility in tasks such as link prediction, node classification, and recommendation. While most embedding techniques strive to preserve specific graph properties in a low-dimensional space, real-world graphs often exhibit complex, multifaceted characteristics that no single method can fully capture.

This paper introduces the novel problem of graph representation ensemble learning and proposes the first framework for efficiently aggregating multiple graph embedding methods. We present a comprehensive analysis of our framework, examining both theoretically and empirically the relationships between various state-of-the-art embedding techniques.

Our models are evaluated on node classification across four real-world graphs. The results demonstrate that our proposed ensemble approaches can surpass existing state-of-the-art methods by up to 8% in macro-F1 score. Furthermore, we show that this approach yields even greater benefits for underrepresented classes, achieving improvements of up to 12%.

This paper introduces a comprehensive framework to rigorously guarantee the performance of the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm and its variant, gradient EM. Our analysis proceeds in two stages: first, we examine these algorithms at the population level (with infinite data), then extend our findings to updates derived from finite sample sets. We begin by characterizing the basin of attraction for any global maximizer of the population likelihood. This characterization stems from a novel perspective: EM updates are viewed as a perturbed form of likelihood ascent, while gradient EM updates are seen as a perturbed form of standard gradient ascent. Building on this, we provide non-asymptotic performance guarantees for both EM and gradient EM when applied to finite samples.
