To address the inherent variability of renewable energy sources, this study employs two established machine learning techniques to predict solar power output from a photovoltaic system. Support vector machines are used to generate individual forecasts, while a random forest acts as an ensemble method to combine these predictions. Unlike common ensemble approaches in renewable energy forecasting that blend meteorological data, this research incorporates present and past solar power forecasts from multiple models, alongside relevant meteorological data, into the random forest. This innovative approach aims to combine and enhance the accuracy of day-ahead solar power forecasts. The efficacy of this combined model is assessed over a full year and benchmarked against alternative combining methodologies.

Deep learning stands as the dominant approach across numerous machine learning applications, such as image recognition, machine translation, and speech recognition. It has consistently surpassed traditional methods, leading to significant breakthroughs. However, the underlying mechanisms of its success are not yet fully understood, highlighting the critical need for a robust theoretical framework.

This work offers a geometric perspective on deep learning, proposing that its effectiveness stems from the inherent manifold structure within data. We posit that high-dimensional natural data tends to cluster around low-dimensional manifolds, and deep learning excels at learning both these manifolds and their associated probability distributions.

We introduce two key concepts: "rectified linear complexity" for deep neural networks, which quantifies their learning capacity, and "rectified linear complexity of an embedding manifold," which gauges the difficulty of learning a given manifold. Our analysis demonstrates that for any deep neural network with a fixed architecture, there will always be a manifold that it cannot learn. Finally, we propose leveraging optimal mass transportation theory to manage the probability distribution within the latent space.

The last ten years have seen significant advancements in the development of new recommender system (RecSys) methods. Despite this progress, the RecSys research community continues to face a core challenge: a shortage of applied datasets and benchmarks, along with clearly defined evaluation rules and metrics, to effectively test these innovative approaches.

To address this gap, we introduce TTRS—the Tinkoff Transactions Recommender System benchmark. This financial transaction dataset comprises over 2 million interactions involving nearly 10,000 users and more than 1,000 merchant brands, recorded over a 14-month period. We believe this to be the first publicly available dataset of its kind.

To enhance its utility for practical applications, we provide a complete account of the data collection pipeline, preprocessing steps, and key dataset statistics. Furthermore, we offer a thorough comparison of popular RecSys methods on the task of next-period recommendation, coupled with a detailed analysis of their performance across various metrics and datasets.

This work introduces and evaluates novel methods for predicting social media users' geographic locations, relevant for health surveillance, emergency monitoring, content personalization, and social studies. Our approach integrates weighted multigraphs with deep learning techniques. We explore methods that, while originating from a shared underlying structure (an extended mention/follower network), employ diverse information processing strategies. These include information diffusion through transductive (RGCNs) and inductive (GraphSAGE) algorithms, and node embeddings using Node2vec+.  Attention mechanisms are then used to combine these graph-based representations with the users' textual data. We assess the performance of these methods against baseline models using the public Twitter-US dataset and a newly created Latin American Twitter dataset. Finally, we discuss the limitations and validity of inter-method comparisons, considering varied label definitions and metrics.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) have garnered significant attention due to their impressive performance in tasks like node classification. Despite this, a comprehensive understanding of their underlying mechanisms, particularly in node representation learning, remains elusive. This paper introduces a theoretical framework to demystify GNNs, focusing on spectral graph convolutional networks and graph attention networks through the lens of graph signal denoising.

Our framework reveals that GNNs implicitly address graph signal denoising challenges: spectral graph convolutions denoise node features, while graph attentions denoise edge weights. We further demonstrate that a linear self-attention mechanism can achieve performance comparable to state-of-the-art graph attention methods.

These theoretical insights paved the way for two novel models: GSDN-F and GSDN-EF, designed for effective application on graphs afflicted by noisy node features and/or noisy edges. We validate our theoretical assertions and the efficacy of our new models through experiments on benchmark datasets. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/fuguoji/GSDN}.

The geometric structure of 3D graphs, defined by their nodes and edges, is vital across numerous applications. Molecular graphs, for instance, demonstrate this well, as their geometry directly impacts properties like reactivity and biological activity. To integrate this geometric information into deep learning for 3D graphs, we introduce three distinct geometric graph representations: positional, angle-geometric, and distance-geometric. As a proof of concept, we apply the distance-geometric representation to geometric graph convolutions. To enable the use of standard graph convolutional networks, we implement a straightforward edge weight/edge distance correlation scheme. The parameters for this scheme can either be fixed using reference data or optimized via Bayesian hyperparameter optimization. Our geometric graph convolutions significantly outperform standard methods on the ESOL and Freesol datasets. This work highlights the feasibility and potential of incorporating geometry, specifically through the distance-geometric graph representation, into deep learning applications involving 3D graphs.

This paper presents a method for applying Operational Space Control (OSC) within a reinforcement learning framework, specifically for Cartesian space control under both joint and Cartesian constraints. Our approach facilitates rapid learning with adjustable degrees of freedom and enables policy transfer to a KUKA LBR iiwa for peg-in-hole tasks without extensive dynamics randomization. Prior to simulation-based learning, we conduct system identification to align the simulation environment with real robot dynamics. The integration of constraints into the OSC controller promotes safe learning on real robots and supports the development of flexible, goal-conditioned policies that transfer seamlessly from simulation to reality.

Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has achieved superhuman performance across many environments, yet these methods are notably inefficient, often requiring far more data than humans to reach satisfactory performance. We introduce Neural Episodic Control (NEC), a DRL agent designed for rapid assimilation and action based on new experiences. NEC employs a semi-tabular value function representation, utilizing a buffer of past experiences that combines slowly evolving state representations with quickly updated value function estimates. Our results demonstrate that NEC learns significantly faster than other leading general-purpose DRL agents across diverse environments.

Achieving $\epsilon$-differential privacy (DP) offers a variety of approaches, but selecting an appropriate $\epsilon$ remains a challenge due to the lack of consensus on a "sufficiently small" value. The optimal $\epsilon$ is also contingent on the specific query and data. This paper proposes a method for calculating $\epsilon$ based on $\delta$, which quantifies an adversary's advantage in probabilistically inferring a specific output property. We model the attacker's objective as a Boolean expression involving guesses about particular attributes, potentially within a defined precision. These combined attributes are presumed to be independent. We further assume that both input and output distributions are characterized by either probability density functions or probability mass functions.

Yes, likely. While supervised deep learning excels in many computer vision tasks, setting performance benchmarks, medical image analysis trails natural image applications. A key factor is the scarcity of well-annotated medical image data for researchers. It's commonly understood that precise and reliable interpretation and labeling of such data demands significant expertise. We frequently observe considerable variability in expert annotations of medical images, both among different experts and by the same expert over time. Despite this, it's widely presumed that novice annotators cannot provide valuable annotations for clinical deep learning models. This work challenges that assumption. We investigate the implications of using a minimally trained novice workforce to annotate a complex medical image dataset. Our study examines the time and cost efficiency of novice annotators, their raw performance against gold-standard expert annotators, and the subsequent impact on the performance of a deep learning segmentation model trained to detect hypoplastic left heart syndrome in fetal ultrasound images.

Machine Learning for Software Engineering (ML4SE) is a burgeoning field dedicated to developing methods that assist programmers. For these methods to be practically useful, they must achieve a sufficient level of quality to genuinely aid, rather than hinder, developers. While advancements in code representation and data collection enhance overall model quality, they often overlook project-specific information.

This work explores how targeting a specific project can improve model quality. We introduce a framework to evaluate quality enhancements gained through fine-tuning, focusing on the method name prediction task for individual projects. We assess three models of varying complexity across three scenarios: training on a large Java project dataset, subsequent fine-tuning with data from a specific project, and training from scratch on that same project's data. Our findings demonstrate that per-project fine-tuning significantly boosts model quality by effectively capturing a project's unique domain and naming conventions. We have open-sourced our data collection tool and experimental code at: https://zenodo.org/record/6040745.

Current industrial robotic assembly is hampered by the need for precise initial conditions, leading to high production costs and limited adaptability. This work addresses these challenges by developing a flexible and adaptable robotic assembly system that leverages 3D CAD models of all components. We demonstrate this approach on the Siemens Innovation Challenge, a task requiring a robot to precisely assemble a gear-like mechanism. To achieve the necessary millimeter-level accuracy for both this task and broader industrial applications, we employ a depth camera positioned near the robot's end-effector. Our method utilizes a high-accuracy, two-stage pose estimation procedure built upon deep convolutional neural networks. This procedure encompasses detection, pose estimation, refinement, and robust handling of both near and full symmetries in parts. The networks are trained using simulated depth images, with strategies in place to ensure successful transfer to real-world robotic operations. We achieved an impressive average pose estimation error of 2.16 millimeters and 0.64 degrees, resulting in a 91% success rate for robotic assembly of randomly distributed parts. To our knowledge, this represents the first complete and highly successful robotic assembly solution for the Siemens Innovation Challenge.

Self-supervised learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for acquiring image representations, circumventing the need for extensive labeled datasets. This approach holds particular promise for underwater robotics, where enhancing perception capabilities, such as sonar image classification, is crucial. The inherent confidentiality and interpretive challenges associated with sonar imaging make the creation of large, publicly accessible labeled datasets for supervised learning difficult.

This work explores the efficacy of three self-supervised learning techniques—RotNet, Denoising Autoencoders, and Jigsaw—in learning robust sonar image representations without human annotation. We evaluate their performance through pre-training and transfer learning on real-world sonar image datasets. Our findings demonstrate that self-supervised pre-training achieves classification performance comparable to supervised pre-training in a few-shot transfer learning setting across all investigated methods.

Code and pre-trained models are available at https://github.com/agrija9/ssl-sonar-images.

Test Input Prioritization (TIP) is a crucial technique for efficiently managing the extensive test datasets typically associated with Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), leading to significant savings in computational and labeling expenses. This is especially relevant for large, deployed systems, where production-observed inputs are often recorded for use as future test or training data. Feng et al. introduced DeepGini, a TIP method noted for its speed and simplicity, demonstrating its superior performance over more complex approaches like neuron and surprise coverage. Our extensive study, encompassing four case studies, eight test datasets, and 32,200 trained models, corroborates their findings. However, our research also reveals that other, equally simple baselines from uncertainty quantification, such as predicted softmax likelihood or the entropy of predicted softmax likelihoods, perform comparably to DeepGini.

We present a new framework for unsupervised object segmentation. Our model learns to segment objects from image collections without human annotation by leveraging the principle that object segments can be locally perturbed against a background without compromising scene realism. Our method involves training a generative model for layered scene representations, comprising a background image, a foreground image, and its mask. These are combined to form a composite image by overlaying the masked foreground onto the background. This generative model is adversarially trained against a discriminator, ensuring the generation of realistic composite images. To ensure the foreground layer represents a distinct object, we introduce random shifts to the foreground image and mask relative to the background in the generative model's output. Since the generator is oblivious to these shifts during generation, it is compelled to produce layered representations that remain realistic despite such perturbations.
