Data augmentation, while extensively explored for classifier improvement, remains largely unexamined for its impact on GANs in image synthesis. This work systematically investigates the efficacy of existing augmentation techniques for GAN training across diverse settings. We offer insights and guidelines for augmenting images for both vanilla GANs and regularized GANs, demonstrating substantial improvements in generated image fidelity. Notably, we discover that vanilla GANs, when augmented with both real and generated images, can achieve generation quality comparable to current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, combining this GAN training with other augmentation-based regularization techniques—such as contrastive loss and consistency regularization—further enhances generated image quality. We achieve new state-of-the-art results for conditional generation on CIFAR-10, utilizing both consistency and contrastive loss as additional regularizations.

Our research focuses on sequential decision-making problems, specifically on maximizing the expected total reward while adhering to an expected total utility constraint. We tackle discounted infinite-horizon optimal control problems within Constrained Markov Decision Processes (constrained MDPs) using the natural policy gradient method.

We introduce a novel Natural Policy Gradient Primal-Dual (NPG-PD) method. This approach updates the primal variable through natural policy gradient ascent and the dual variable via projected sub-gradient descent. Despite the non-concave objective function and non-convex constraint set, we prove that our method, when employing softmax policy parametrization, achieves global convergence with sublinear rates for both optimality gap and constraint violation. This convergence is notably dimension-free, meaning it is independent of the state-action space size.

Furthermore, for log-linear and general smooth policy parametrizations, we demonstrate sublinear convergence rates, accounting for a function approximation error stemming from restricted policy parametrization. We also provide convergence and finite-sample complexity guarantees for two sample-based NPG-PD algorithms. Computational experiments validate the effectiveness and advantages of our approach.

High-throughput mRNA sequencing (RNA-Seq) is a common method for quantifying gene isoform transcripts. However, RNA-Seq data alone often falls short in accurately identifying read origins for precise quantification. To address this, we propose integrating protein domain-domain interactions as prior knowledge with RNA-Seq data. Our novel method, Network-based RNA-Seq-based Transcript Quantification (Net-RSTQ), combines a protein domain-domain interaction network with short read alignments to estimate transcript abundance.

We observed a positive correlation between the abundances of isoforms that share domain-domain interactions within the network. Building on this, Net-RSTQ models the expression of neighboring transcripts as Dirichlet priors, which are applied to the likelihood of observed read alignments against transcripts from the same gene. The transcript abundances for all genes are then jointly estimated through an alternating optimization of multiple Expectation-Maximization (EM) problems.

In simulations, Net-RSTQ significantly improved isoform transcript quantification, particularly when isoform co-expression correlated with their interactions. Further validation through qRT-PCR on 25 multi-isoform genes across stem cell, ovarian cancer, and breast cancer cell lines demonstrated that Net-RSTQ provided more consistent isoform proportions when integrated with RNA-Seq data. Experiments using RNA-Seq data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) also revealed improved transcript abundances.

Reinforcement Learning (RL) can be framed as a sequence modeling problem where, given past experiences (state, action, reward), a model autoregressively predicts future actions. While Transformers have shown promise in this area, we introduce the State-Action-Reward Transformer (StARformer) to enhance action prediction in long sequences by explicitly modeling local causal relations.

StARformer operates by first extracting "StAR-representations"—local representations derived from state-action-reward tokens within short time spans. These local representations, combined with state representations, then enable action predictions over extended periods.

Our experiments demonstrate that StARformer surpasses current state-of-the-art Transformer-based methods on both Atari (image) and Gym (state vector) benchmarks, across offline-RL and imitation learning scenarios. Furthermore, StARformer exhibits improved performance with longer input sequences compared to baselines. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/elicassion/StARformer.

This paper introduces Perturbed Convolution (PConv), a new convolutional layer designed to simultaneously enhance Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) performance and mitigate the discriminator's memorization of training data. PConv operates by randomly perturbing the input tensor before the convolution operation, a simple yet remarkably effective approach. This perturbation encourages the discriminator to learn robust features with small local Lipschitz values, enabling consistent output despite input variations. Furthermore, by introducing random perturbations during training, similar to dropout, PConv helps alleviate the memorization problem. We demonstrate PConv's generalization ability through extensive experiments across various loss functions and datasets, including CIFAR-10, CelebA, CelebA-HQ, LSUN, and tiny-ImageNet. Quantitative evaluations show that PConv significantly improves the Frechet Inception Distance (FID) of both GANs and conditional GANs.

Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC) is a widely used method for likelihood-free inference across various disciplines. Its effectiveness hinges on selecting highly performant summary statistics, a process often relying on extensive domain expertise and meticulous feature engineering, making it a time-consuming endeavor. Given ABC's sensitivity to data dimensionality, this selection requires a careful balance between including informative statistics and managing the feature vector's size.

This paper introduces a novel approach: framing the dynamic selection of an appropriate summary statistic from a pool of candidates as a multi-armed bandit problem. This enables ABC rejection sampling to adaptively focus on a distribution of effective summary statistics, rather than being confined to a static set. Our method stands out by requiring no pre-processing and scaling efficiently to a large number of candidate statistics. This allows for the effective utilization of extensive time series summary statistic libraries without prior feature engineering. We benchmark our proposed approach against leading summary statistic selection methods, using a demanding problem from systems biology to demonstrate its efficacy.

This study examines the assumption that identifying and removing code smells improves code quality. We propose characteristics that causal code smells should possess and evaluate 151 smells using CheckStyle on 31,687 Java files from 677 GitHub repositories (all with 200+ commits in 2019). We measured their impact on quality, productivity, and bug detection. Our findings indicate that less than 20% of the analyzed smells are potentially causal, with only a few showing robust correlation. The most impactful smells relate to simplicity, defensive programming, and abstraction. Files free of these potentially causal smells are 50% more likely to be high-quality. However, developers often remove less effective, easier-to-fix smells rather than the more impactful ones.

Our research introduces an efficient computational framework designed to significantly accelerate various machine learning algorithms while preserving accuracy. This framework leverages projections performed by "Structured Spinners"—matrices formed from the product of three structured, rotation-incorporating blocks.

The framework's versatility is a key advantage:
*   **Flexible Matrix Construction:** Structured matrices can be either entirely randomized or learned.
*   **Comprehensive Coverage:** Our structured family encompasses all previously investigated structured schemes as special cases.
*   **Non-linear Extension:** The approach extends to non-linear scenarios where projections are followed by non-linear functions.
*   **Broad Applicability:** The method has numerous applications, including kernel approximations via random feature maps, dimensionality reduction, novel fast cross-polytope LSH techniques, deep learning, convex optimization via Newton sketches, and quantization using random projection trees.

We provide theoretical guarantees that characterize the capacity of our structured model in relation to its unstructured equivalent, grounded in a general theoretical principle detailed in the paper. As a direct outcome of our analysis, we offer the first theoretical guarantees for the highly efficient LSH algorithm that utilizes the HD3HD2HD1 structured matrix [Andoni et al., 2015]. Extensive experimental validation confirms its effectiveness.

We introduce a novel training methodology for deep neural networks (DNNs), enabling them to operate with arbitrary precision during inference. This approach yields a single DNN model that can dynamically adjust its numerical precision at runtime by truncating least significant bits, thus offering a flexible trade-off between speed and accuracy. Our experiments demonstrate that when all layers are configured for low-bit precision, the model maintains accuracy comparable to models specifically trained for that precision.

This adaptability simplifies the deployment of deep learning models in real-world scenarios, where a balance between accuracy and computational efficiency is frequently required. Unlike prior work that focuses on training discrete models for each specific efficiency/accuracy point, our method addresses the largely unexplored challenge of creating models inherently flexible in runtime precision. This is particularly advantageous when efficiency and accuracy demands fluctuate, as it eliminates the impracticality of retraining or storing numerous models. Our framework achieves this flexibility without compromising performance and is broadly applicable across various model architectures and vision tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/SHI-Labs/Any-Precision-DNNs.

We study the problem of identifying the largest community within a population by sequentially sampling individuals. The population is divided into communities and also into "boxes," which are distinct sampling domains. Individuals from various communities may be present in any given box, and conversely, a single community can span multiple boxes.

Our learning agent can repeatedly sample (with replacement) a random individual from any chosen box. Upon sampling, the agent learns the individual's community and whether they have been sampled previously. The agent's objective is to minimize the probability of incorrectly identifying the largest community within a fixed budget, achieved by optimizing both its sampling strategy and decision-making process.

We introduce and analyze new algorithms for this problem. Additionally, we derive information-theoretic lower bounds on the error probability for any algorithm. For several relevant scenarios, our algorithms' error probabilities exhibit exponential decay rates that are optimal within a constant factor. We further validate our proposed algorithms through simulations using real-world datasets.

Rectified Linear Units (ReLUs) are the favored activation function in artificial neural networks. This paper investigates two fundamental learning problems, assuming the data originate from a generative model based on a ReLU-network (a neural network employing ReLU activations). As a theoretical exploration, we focus on a single-layer network.

The first problem addresses dictionary learning with nonlinearity, specifically modeled by ReLU functions. Given observation vectors $\mathbf{y}^i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ for $i =1, 2, \dots , n$, our goal is to recover a $d\times k$ matrix $A$ and latent vectors $\{\mathbf{c}^i\} \subset \mathbb{R}^k$ based on the model $\mathbf{y}^i = \mathrm{ReLU}(A\mathbf{c}^i +\mathbf{b})$, where $\mathbf{b}\in \mathbb{R}^d$ is a random bias. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions on the probability distribution of $\mathbf{b}$, the column space of $A$ can be recovered with an error of $O(d)$ (in Frobenius norm).

The second problem concerns the robust recovery of a signal amidst outliers, interpreted as significant but sparse noise. Here, we aim to recover the latent vector $\mathbf{c}$ from its noisy nonlinear sketches, which take the form $\mathbf{v} = \mathrm{ReLU}(A\mathbf{c}) + \mathbf{e}+\mathbf{w}$, where $\mathbf{e} \in \mathbb{R}^d$.

Our data-driven approach constructs uncertainty sets for robust optimization problems. We model uncertain parameters as random variables with an unknown joint probability distribution. Using only independent samples from this distribution, we develop a nonparametric method to estimate uncertainty sets. This method guarantees that the probability mass of these sets approximates a target mass within a given tolerance, with high confidence. The nonparametric estimators we use also exhibit distribution-free finite-sample performance bounds, ensuring their convergence in probability to the target mass. These estimators are computationally efficient and produce uncertainty sets that lead to computationally tractable robust optimization problems for a wide range of constraint functions.

Drawing inspiration from the LISTA algorithm, we propose a versatile neural network architecture tailored for sparse reconstruction from limited linear measurements. This framework accommodates diverse neural network types, from recurrent to feedforward, by allowing varying degrees of weight-sharing across layers, facilitating a unified analytical approach. Our objective is to learn optimal network parameters and, consequently, an optimal network for signal reconstruction from low-dimensional linear measurements, achieved through empirical risk minimization on training samples. We establish generalization bounds by analyzing the Rademacher complexity of hypothesis classes comprising these deep networks, incorporating thresholding parameters into our analysis. Our sample complexity estimates exhibit an approximate linear dependence on the number of parameters and depth. We then apply our findings to derive specific generalization bounds for various practical applications, including implicit dictionary learning algorithms and convolutional neural networks.

Comparing the top $k$ elements of ranked lists is a frequent task, yet existing measures, despite their mathematical elegance, often fall short in practice. This paper introduces a novel information-theoretic measure for comparing any two top $k$ lists. Our method assesses list compressibility, using the lossless encoding length as a natural and robust indicator of variability. This information-theoretic approach objectively addresses key considerations in list similarity: the proportion of non-overlapping elements, the disarray among overlapping elements, and the displacement of actual ranks for overlapping elements.

Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is widely used for non-convex optimization, despite its conventional convergence theory indicating a slow sublinear approach to a stationary point. This work presents new convergence theorems for SGD, demonstrating its ability to reach a global minimum for non-convex problems under specific structural conditions. We concentrate on two significant categories of structured non-convex functions: Quasar (Strongly) Convex functions, which generalize convex functions, and functions satisfying the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition, a broader form of strongly-convex functions. Our analysis introduces an "Expected Residual condition," which we prove is less restrictive than prior assumptions like growth conditions, expected smoothness, or bounded variance. We offer theoretical assurances for SGD's convergence across various step-size strategies, including constant, decreasing, and the novel stochastic Polyak step-size. Furthermore, our analysis is applicable to any sampling method, providing insights into minibatching complexity and identifying an optimal minibatch size. We also show that for models capable of interpolating training data, our Expected Residual condition can be omitted, yielding state-of-the-art results.

Data imbalance often hinders neural network classification. We introduce Discriminative Feature Generation (DFG), a novel supervised method for minority class datasets. DFG adapts a Generative Adversarial Network with a generator, discriminator, feature extractor, and classifier. To augment minority class data with discriminative features, the generator is trained using an attention mechanism for the class-imbalanced task, while the feature extractor and classifier are regularized with pre-trained features from a large source dataset. Our experiments demonstrate that the DFG generator effectively augments label-preserving and diverse features, significantly improving classification performance on the target task. This method promises substantial contributions to data augmentation through discriminative feature generation and supervised attention.

We investigate the problem of identifying the optimal arm in a stochastic multi-armed bandit setting. We are given $n$ arms, each with an unknown reward distribution on $[0,1]$, characterized by mean $\theta_i$ and variance $\sigma_i^2$. We assume $\theta_1 > \theta_2 \geq \cdots \geq\theta_n$. Our proposed adaptive algorithm, based on a novel "grouped median elimination" approach, strategically explores reward gaps and variances to inform future decisions. This algorithm guarantees identification of the best arm with probability $(1-\delta)$ using at most $O \left(\sum_{i = 1}^n \left(\frac{\sigma_i^2}{\Delta_i^2} + \frac{1}{\Delta_i}\right)(\ln \delta^{-1} + \ln \ln \Delta_i^{-1})\right)$ samples, where $\Delta_i$ (for $i \geq 2$) represents the reward gap between arm $i$ and the best arm, and $\Delta_1 = \Delta_2$. This significantly outperforms variance-independent algorithms in certain scenarios and, notably, is the first result to eliminate the $\ln n$ factor previously observed in state-of-the-art methods regarding the best arm. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a lower bound of $\Omega \left( \sum_{i = 1}^n \left( \frac{\sigma_i^2}{\Delta_i^2} + \frac{1}{\Delta_i} \right) \ln \delta^{-1} \right)$ samples is necessary to achieve this objective, thereby illustrating the efficiency of our approach.

Belief Propagation (BP) is a cornerstone message-passing algorithm used for probabilistic reasoning and inference within graphical models. While its exactness on tree-structured graphs is established, BP is frequently applied to graphs containing cycles, leading to what is known as "loopy" BP. Deciphering the behavior of loopy BP has posed a significant challenge in machine learning research. Existing positive convergence guarantees for BP typically rely on strong assumptions, often implying that the underlying graphical model exhibits correlation decay.

We demonstrate that, from a natural initialization, BP rapidly converges to the global optimum of the Bethe free energy for ferromagnetic Ising models on any graph. This holds even when such models display long-range correlations and may possess multiple suboptimal BP fixed points. Ferromagnetic models are characterized by a preference for alignment between neighboring spins. Furthermore, we present a similar finding for iterative solutions to the naive mean-field equations. Remarkably, both results are "dimension-free," meaning that a fixed, small number of iterations suffices to provide an accurate estimate of the Bethe or mean-field free energy.

This paper introduces a novel 2-order graphic neighbor information feature extraction method, building upon the existing 1-order approach, to improve the accuracy of protein-protein interaction function prediction. This method, based on undirected simple graphs, also incorporates the chi-square test for feature combination. To validate the efficacy of our 2-order graphic neighbor features, we evaluated four logistic regression models—LR, DKLR, PKLR, and RBF KLR—across two distinct feature sets. Experiments conducted on protein-protein interaction data from the Munich Information Center for Protein Sequences (MIPS) for protein function prediction within the Yeast Proteome Database (YPD) demonstrate that leveraging 2-order graphic neighbor information significantly boosts the average overall percentage of protein function prediction, particularly when using RBF KLR. Furthermore, employing a new 5-top chi-square feature combination method, RBF KLR achieved an impressive 99.05% average overall percentage on the 2-order neighbor feature combination set.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) offer a powerful machine-learning approach for solving and identifying partial differential equations (PDEs). This work applies PINNs to solve the Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) equations for incompressible turbulent flows. Notably, our method does not rely on specific turbulence models or assumptions and utilizes only boundary data.

We first demonstrate PINNs' efficacy in solving the Navier-Stokes equations for laminar flows using the Falkner-Skan boundary layer as an example. Subsequently, we apply PINNs to simulate four turbulent flow scenarios: a zero-pressure-gradient boundary layer, an adverse-pressure-gradient boundary layer, and turbulent flows over a NACA4412 airfoil and a periodic hill.

Our findings indicate that PINNs are exceptionally well-suited for laminar flows with significant pressure gradients, achieving predictions with less than 1% error. Furthermore, for turbulent flows, our simulations demonstrate very high accuracy, extending even to the Reynolds-stress components.

Deep convolutional networks excel at image classification. Current methods for explaining their predictions often use gradient-based saliency maps, which highlight the entire foreground object. However, humans typically interpret images by identifying and combining smaller, more specific concepts. We introduce MACE: a Model Agnostic Concept Extractor, designed to explain convolutional network behavior through these granular concepts. MACE analyzes a convolutional network's feature maps to extract concept-based, prototypical explanations. Crucially, it also quantifies the relevance of these concepts to the model's specific class predictions—a capability absent in existing approaches. We validate MACE using VGG16 and ResNet50 architectures on datasets such as Animals With Attributes 2 (AWA2) and Places365. Our experiments show that MACE's extracted concepts significantly improve the human interpretability and fidelity of the explanations for the underlying black-box models.

This paper introduces a modified neural network model designed to simulate Markov Chains. We detail its architecture and training methodology, demonstrating how to imbue it with statistical properties derived from training data. We showcase several applications where the network generates non-deterministic outcomes, including a random walker model applicable to Brownian motion simulations, and a Tic-Tac-Toe network that exhibits non-deterministic game play.

Deep learning has yielded a variety of architectures for time series analysis, adaptable to diverse datasets and domains. This article examines common encoder and decoder designs for both one-step-ahead and multi-horizon forecasting, detailing their methods for integrating temporal information into predictions. We then explore recent advancements in hybrid deep learning models, which merge established statistical techniques with neural networks to enhance the performance of individual methods. Finally, we discuss how deep learning can support decision-making processes involving time series data.

Deep learning's rapid advancements are making video forgeries increasingly effortless and affordable to produce. This underscores the critical need for dependable forgery detection methods. This paper introduces such an approach, applicable across various tampering scenarios. We frame the problem as a per-frame binary classification. To enhance tampering detection across diverse facial manipulation scenarios, we propose leveraging transfer learning from face recognition. Furthermore, in low-resolution contexts where single-frame detection falters, we explore utilizing neighboring frames to classify the middle frame. Both approaches are evaluated on the public FaceForensics benchmark, where they achieve state-of-the-art accuracy.

This paper analyzes character-level machine translation models within pivot-based translation, specifically their application to sparse and noisy datasets like crowdsourced movie subtitles. Our experiments show that these models reduce untranslated words by over 40% and offer significant improvements (2-3 BLEU points) with limited training data. We investigate how character alignment, phrase table filtering, bitext size, and pivot language choice affect translation quality. We also compare cascaded translation models with synthetic training data generated through multiple pivots, finding the latter to be superior. Finally, we highlight that neither word- nor character-BLEU perfectly aligns with human judgments due to BLEU's length sensitivity.

Femtosecond- to attosecond-duration laser pulses are the shortest events ever generated. Their characterization (amplitude and phase) is crucial for ultrafast science applications, such as studying chemical reactions and electronic phase transitions. We present the first deep neural network technique for reconstructing ultra-short optical pulses, demonstrated through numerical simulations and experiments. This method is expected to broaden the scope of ultrashort pulse characterization, enabling the diagnosis of even very weak attosecond pulses.

Previous face recognition algorithms exhibited racial bias, performing with varying accuracy across different racial groups. This paper explores the potential causes of this bias, categorizing them into data-driven factors and scenario modeling factors, and outlines methodological approaches for its assessment. Data-driven factors include image quality, population statistics of image datasets, and algorithmic architecture. Scenario modeling factors consider the influence of the algorithm's user, such as threshold decisions and demographic constraints.

We illustrate these concepts using data from four face recognition algorithms: one earlier-generation algorithm and three deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs), evaluated on East Asian and Caucasian faces. Our findings indicate three key points:

1.  **Dataset difficulty influenced both overall accuracy and racial bias:** As the difficulty of the dataset increased, so did the observed racial bias.
2.  **Bias varied with identification decision thresholds:** For all four algorithms, the extent of bias was dependent on the threshold set for identification decisions. To achieve equivalent false accept rates (FARs), East Asian faces consistently required higher identification thresholds than Caucasian faces across all algorithms.
3.  **Demographic constraints impacted accuracy estimates:** How demographic distributions were formulated for testing significantly affected the estimated accuracy of the algorithms.

In conclusion, we assert that racial bias requires application-specific measurement. We provide a checklist to guide the assessment of racial bias in face recognition algorithms.

sktime is an open-source, Python-based toolkit for time series analysis. Developed by researchers at the University of East Anglia (UEA), University College London, and the Alan Turing Institute, it is designed to be compatible with scikit-learn.

Initially, a primary objective for sktime was to offer time series classification features on par with those found in tsml, a related Java package also developed at UEA. This paper details the implementation of six such classifiers within sktime and compares them to their tsml counterparts.

We demonstrate their correctness by comparing their accuracy across various standard test problems. Additionally, we compare the build times of the different implementations. Our findings indicate a significant accuracy difference in only one of the six algorithms examined: Proximity Forest, a discrepancy that is currently a source of debugging challenges. We observed a much wider range of differences in efficiency. While not unexpected, these disparities highlight potential areas for improvement in both toolkits.

Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs), inspired by biological neural functions, are a class of learning systems often employing Hebbian learning principles like "neurons that wire together, fire together." Unlike their biological counterparts, ANNs inherently exhibit a rigid coupling between their neuronal modules. This interconnectedness imposes an inflexible structure, preventing weight updates until a complete forward and backward pass has been executed. While this constraint might have been acceptable in the past, it has become impractical in the era of very-large-scale machine learning, especially with the growing demand for parallelizing the learning process across distributed computing infrastructures.

To address this limitation, synthetic gradients (SG) combined with decoupled neural interfaces (DNI) offer a promising alternative to traditional backpropagation. This paper benchmarks the speed and accuracy of SG-DNI against a standard neural interface using a multilayer perceptron (MLP). The results demonstrate that SG-DNI effectively solves the learning problem and is over three times faster due to its asynchronous learning capabilities.

Greedy algorithms excel at maximizing monotone submodular functions but struggle with non-monotonicity.  Surprisingly, we demonstrate that repeatedly applying the classical greedy algorithm $O(\sqrt{k})$-times, in a method we call Repeated Greedy, yields the fastest known deterministic algorithm for maximizing general submodular functions under $k$-independent system constraints. Repeated Greedy achieves a $(1 + O(1/\sqrt{k}))k$ approximation with $O(nr\sqrt{k})$ function evaluations, where $n$ is the ground set size and $r$ is the maximum feasible solution size.

Furthermore, we introduce Sample Greedy, the fastest known randomized algorithm for maximizing submodular functions subject to $k$-extendible system constraints (a subset of $k$-independent system constraints). By employing a careful sampling procedure, Sample Greedy achieves a $(k + 3)$-approximation with only $O(nr/k)$ function evaluations using a single run of the greedy algorithm.

We establish a nearly matching lower bound, proving that no polynomial-time algorithm can achieve an approximation ratio better than $k + 1/2 - \varepsilon$. Our theoretical findings are corroborated by empirical comparisons of Repeated Greedy and Sample Greedy against existing methods in a real-world application (movie recommendation).

This paper introduces three novel error bounds for covariance estimation under differential privacy, measured by the Frobenius norm:

1.  A worst-case bound of $\tilde{O}(d^{1/4}/\sqrt{n})$, which outperforms the standard Gaussian mechanism's $\tilde{O}(d/n)$ in scenarios where $d>\widetilde{\Omega}(n^{2/3})$.
2.  A trace-sensitive bound that achieves a $\sqrt{d}$-factor improvement over existing methods.
3.  A tail-sensitive bound that provides more instance-specific results.

The algorithms associated with these bounds are straightforward and efficient. Experimental validation demonstrates substantial improvements over previous research.

Communication in parallel systems often creates a significant bottleneck in parallel machine learning due to substantial overhead. To mitigate this, we introduce EventGraD, an event-triggered communication algorithm for stochastic gradient descent in parallel machine learning. Unlike standard implementations that require communication at every iteration, EventGraD communicates only when necessary, at specific iterations. We provide a theoretical convergence analysis for our algorithm. Furthermore, we demonstrate EventGraD's effectiveness by implementing it for data-parallel training of a residual neural network on the CIFAR-10 dataset. Our results show that EventGraD can reduce communication load by up to 60% without compromising accuracy. EventGraD can also be integrated with other techniques, such as Top-K sparsification, to further decrease communication while maintaining accuracy.

Standard statistical inference and machine learning generalization bounds assume that tests are conducted on data selected independently of the hypotheses. However, practical data analysis and machine learning often involve iterative and adaptive processes, where the same holdout data is repeatedly used to test a sequence of hypotheses or models. Each subsequent test may depend on the outcomes of previous tests on the same data.

In this paper, we introduce RadaBound, a rigorous, efficient, and practical procedure designed to control generalization error when a holdout sample is used for multiple adaptive tests. Our approach leverages a novel application of Rademacher Complexity generalization bounds, specifically adapted for dependent tests. We demonstrate RadaBound's statistical power and practical utility through extensive simulations and comparisons with alternative methods.

Biology serves as a crucial domain for applying and inspiring advanced machine learning techniques. While high-throughput sequencing has garnered significant attention for generating large, complex datasets, high-quality video recording technology now produces similarly rich data demanding sophisticated computer vision and time-series analysis methods. Furthermore, just as studying gene expression in one organism can unveil universal biological principles, examining intricate social interactions in an experimentally controlled system like a laboratory ant colony can illuminate general dynamics applicable to other social groups. This paper focuses on one such instance: investigating reproductive regulation in small laboratory colonies of over 50 Harpegnathos ants. These ants can be artificially prompted to undergo a roughly 20-day hierarchy reformation process. Although the culmination of this process is evident to human observers, the specific behaviors contributing to it during the transitional period remain largely unknown. To shed light on this, we explore the potential of One-class Classification (OC) for identifying abnormal states in ant colonies, particularly when behavioral data is limited.

The growing volume of healthcare data necessitates efficient tools for data-driven medicine. We present a distributed system that utilizes Stratified Locality Sensitive Hashing for rapid, similarity-based predictions on extensive medical waveform datasets. Designed for cloud environments and prioritizing low latency over high throughput, our system is demonstrated in an ICU setting for predicting Acute Hypotensive Episodes from Arterial Blood Pressure waveforms. When applied to a dataset of 1.37 million points, our system scales effectively across up to 40 processors, achieving a 21-fold reduction in comparisons compared to parallel exhaustive search, with only a 10% decrease in Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC). Greater speedups, up to two orders of magnitude, are attainable if further MCC loss is acceptable.

The global COVID-19 pandemic presents novel challenges for researchers. Artificial intelligence (AI) can help predict epidemic parameters, risks, and effects, aiding in disease control and prevention. However, applying AI is difficult due to limited and uncertain data. We propose a shallow LSTM-based neural network to predict a country's risk category. Using Bayesian optimization, we designed and optimized country-specific networks. Our method surpasses existing approaches for 180 countries, proving valuable for risk categorization. We also found that weather data does not significantly improve predictions when combined with trend data. This tool can forecast long-term outbreaks, enabling proactive prevention.

Machine learning with molecules is difficult because their natural representation is as graphs, not vectors. While several deep learning architectures for molecular graphs have emerged, they face information bottlenecks by limiting information flow to direct neighbors. Our new method, Graph Informer, overcomes this by introducing a more expressive route-based multi-attention mechanism that incorporates features from paths between node pairs. This allows a single network layer to consider nodes multiple steps away. Empirically, Graph Informer outperforms existing methods in two prediction tasks: improving the state-of-the-art for 13C Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectra with a Mean Absolute Error of 1.35 ppm, and predicting drug bioactivity and toxicity. We also developed an injective variant of Graph Informer, which is provably as powerful as the Weisfeiler-Lehman test for graph isomorphism. Moreover, we show that Graph Informer's use of route information enables it to understand the nonlocal topology of the graph, exceeding the capabilities of the Weisfeiler-Lehman test.

Many data types in data mining, such as terms and documents, customer purchases, or movie reviews, can be represented as bipartite graphs. This paper introduces a novel data clustering method that partitions these graphs. Our method minimizes the normalized sum of edge weights between unmatched vertex pairs to achieve this partition. We show that a partial singular value decomposition (SVD) of the bipartite graph's edge weight matrix provides an approximate solution to this minimization. We also highlight the link between our algorithm and correspondence analysis and discuss assigning data objects to multiple clusters. Finally, we demonstrate our algorithm's effectiveness and efficiency through document clustering experiments.

Deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) holds great promise for robotic control, enabling the learning of policies for complex, unmodeled systems with high-dimensional, continuous control. However, the field of Robotic RL currently suffers from a lack of clearly defined benchmark tasks, hindering reproducibility and comparative analysis. While "Reacher" tasks are frequently used as benchmarks for robotic manipulation, their informal specifications often omit crucial details necessary for replication. This paper presents a novel empirical analysis demonstrating that unstated spatial constraints in common Reacher task implementations significantly simplify the learning of successful control policies using Deep Deterministic Policy Gradients (DDPG), a state-of-the-art Deep RL algorithm. Our findings suggest that less constrained Reacher tasks are considerably more challenging to learn, indicating that existing de facto benchmarks may not accurately reflect the true difficulty of general robotic manipulation.

We introduce a new Stochastic Frank-Wolfe (conditional gradient) algorithm for constrained, smooth, finite-sum minimization problems, particularly those with generalized linear prediction/structure. This encompasses applications like empirical risk minimization with sparse or low-rank constraints. Our method offers easy implementation, eliminates the need for step-size tuning, and maintains a constant per-iteration cost regardless of dataset size. Additionally, it yields a stochastic estimator of the Frank-Wolfe gap, suitable for use as a stopping criterion. The algorithm's computational guarantees either match or surpass existing Stochastic Frank-Wolfe methods, depending on the specific context. Empirical evaluations across various datasets demonstrate its faster convergence in certain scenarios compared to related approaches. An open-source package containing implementations of all discussed methods is also provided.

The existing literature lacks exploration into knowledge transfer across multiple streaming processes, an area characterized by unique challenges: the absence of labeled instances in the target domain, covariate shift between source and target domains, and differing drift periods. To address this, we propose Autonomous Transfer Learning (ATL), a flexible deep learning approach designed for online unsupervised transfer learning across numerous streaming processes. ATL employs an online domain adaptation strategy, integrating generative and discriminative phases with KL divergence-based optimization to create a domain-invariant network. A key feature is its elastic network structure, which autonomously evolves from scratch, with or without ground truth, to manage independent concept drifts in both source and target domains. Rigorous numerical evaluations and comparisons with recent works demonstrate ATL's superior performance and significantly faster training speed compared to existing methods.

Machine learning models are susceptible to data-poisoning attacks, where malicious actors manipulate training data to alter model predictions. These attacks manifest in two primary forms: trigger-less attacks, where attackers can modify the training set but not test inputs, and backdoor attacks, which additionally allow attackers to modify test inputs. Current model-agnostic defense strategies either fail to address backdoor attacks or lack robust certifications of their effectiveness.

We introduce BagFlip, a certified, model-agnostic defense designed to counter both trigger-less and backdoor attacks. We demonstrate BagFlip's efficacy through evaluations on image classification and malware detection datasets. Our results show that BagFlip performs comparably to or surpasses state-of-the-art methods against trigger-less attacks, and it demonstrably outperforms existing approaches in defending against backdoor attacks.

Mouse dynamics offer a promising avenue for user authentication. While traditional methods rely on classical machine learning, deep learning approaches have recently emerged. Despite demonstrated vulnerabilities of machine learning and deep learning to adversarial attacks, research into adversarial behavioral biometrics remains limited. To address this gap, we developed several generative attacks that craft adversarial mouse trajectories to bypass authentication models. These generated sequences serve as our adversarial samples. We analyze the limitations of our attack approaches. Unlike previous work, our attacks operate in a more realistic and challenging scenario where the attacker has access to user data but not the authentication model or its outputs. We explore three attack strategies—statistics-based, imitation-based, and surrogate-based—and demonstrate their effectiveness in evading authentication models, thereby compromising their robustness.

Federated learning enables the training of machine learning models across distributed datasets without direct data sharing.  Within this paradigm, vertical federated learning addresses scenarios where data sources share common sample IDs but possess distinct feature sets.  Sustaining participant engagement hinges on fairly evaluating and compensating each data source's contribution.

The Shapley value (SV), derived from cooperative game theory, offers a demonstrably fair method for assessing contributions. However, its computation typically demands numerous model re-trainings on various data source subsets, leading to prohibitive communication overheads in federated learning environments.

To overcome this, we introduce the Vertical Federated Shapley Value (VerFedSV), a novel contribution valuation metric building upon the SV. We demonstrate that VerFedSV retains the desirable fairness properties of SV while offering computational efficiency. Furthermore, VerFedSV is adaptable to both synchronous and asynchronous vertical federated learning algorithms. Our theoretical analysis and comprehensive experimental results confirm VerFedSV's fairness, efficiency, and adaptability.

A core tenet of Bayesian methods is marginalization, contrasting with the single-point estimates of traditional approaches. This marginalization can significantly boost the accuracy and calibration of deep neural networks, which often suffer from underspecification and can converge to multiple distinct, yet plausible, solutions. Our work demonstrates that deep ensembles serve as an effective approximation of Bayesian marginalization. We introduce a novel, low-overhead approach that further refines the predictive distribution by marginalizing within basins of attraction.

We also explore the functional prior implied by diffuse neural network weight distributions, offering a probabilistic explanation for their generalization capabilities. This perspective demystifies previously perplexing neural network phenomena, such as their capacity to fit randomly labeled images, showing these behaviors are reproducible with Gaussian processes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Bayesian model averaging mitigates double descent, leading to consistent performance gains with increased model flexibility. Lastly, we offer a Bayesian interpretation of tempering for calibrating predictive distributions.

Building on MacKay (1992), we contend that standard model-based active learning methods, such as BALD, suffer from a critical flaw: they overlook the test-time distribution of input variables. This oversight can compromise the acquisition strategy, as information maximizing for model parameters may not be for prediction. This is particularly true when the pool data is more dispersed than the final prediction task, or when pool and test sample distributions diverge. To address this, we propose an acquisition strategy that maximizes the expected information gain about future predictions, which we term Expected Predictive Information Gain (EPIG). Recognizing EPIG's limited scalability for batch acquisition, we also explore a hybrid approach combining BALD and EPIG, called Joint Expected Predictive Information Gain (JEPIG). We evaluate both strategies for active learning with Bayesian neural networks across various datasets, specifically analyzing their performance under distribution shift within the pool set.

Recent years have seen a surge in interest surrounding video action recognition systems. However, direct comparisons of accuracy and computational performance are often hindered by variations in training environments, hardware, hyperparameters, pipelines, and inference methods. This article addresses this challenge by providing a consistent, head-to-head comparison of fourteen off-the-shelf and state-of-the-art models. We evaluate model accuracy using standard Top-1 and Top-5 metrics, alongside a newly proposed metric. Furthermore, we analyze the computational performance of distributed training across two to sixty-four GPUs on a cutting-edge HPC system.

Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) seeks to transfer knowledge from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain. Current UDA methods primarily utilize Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) to learn domain-invariant feature representations at either the domain or category level. A significant challenge for category-level UDA is the generation of accurate pseudo-labels for target domain samples, as noisy labels often compromise domain alignment and, consequently, UDA performance.

Leveraging the success of Transformers, we observe that their cross-attention mechanism effectively handles noisy input pairs, leading to superior feature alignment. Therefore, this paper proposes a Transformer-based approach for the demanding UDA task. To improve the accuracy of input pairs, we introduce a two-way center-aware labeling algorithm for generating pseudo-labels for target samples.

Furthermore, we propose a weight-sharing triple-branch Transformer framework. This framework employs self-attention for learning source and target features and cross-attention for aligning source and target domains. This design explicitly encourages the simultaneous learning of discriminative domain-specific and domain-invariant representations. Our method, named CDTrans (Cross-Domain Transformer), represents a pioneering effort in addressing UDA tasks using a pure Transformer architecture.

Probabilistic hierarchical time-series forecasting is a critical area within time-series analysis, focusing on modeling and predicting multivariate time series structured by hierarchical relationships. While many existing methods offer point predictions, they often lack well-calibrated probabilistic forecast distributions. Even recent state-of-the-art probabilistic forecasting approaches typically impose hierarchical constraints on point predictions or sampled distributions, neglecting the crucial aspect of forecast distribution coherency. Furthermore, prior research frequently assumes, often implicitly, that datasets perfectly conform to given hierarchical relations, failing to address real-world data inconsistencies.

This paper introduces PROFHIT, a novel model designed to address these limitations. PROFHIT is a fully probabilistic hierarchical forecasting model that jointly models the forecast distribution across the entire hierarchy. It employs a flexible probabilistic Bayesian framework and incorporates a new Distributional Coherency regularization. This regularization enables PROFHIT to learn from hierarchical relationships across the entire forecast distribution, resulting in robust and calibrated forecasts that can adapt to datasets with varying degrees of hierarchical consistency. Empirical evaluations of PROFHIT across a diverse set of datasets demonstrate a 41-88% improvement in accuracy and calibration. By modeling coherency across the full distribution, PROFHIT also proves capable of providing reliable forecasts even with up to 10% missing input time-series data.

The healthcare system increasingly mandates wearable devices for remote data collection and real-time health monitoring. This adoption dramatically increases data volume. However, the high processing demands for data collection and transmission quickly deplete the small batteries of these devices. Given the criticality of medical data, all transmitted information must meet strict integrity and availability standards.

To extend device battery life, this paper proposes using an inference algorithm to reduce healthcare data volume and transmission frequency. While improving transmission metrics often presents a trade-off between accuracy and efficiency (where increased accuracy typically reduces efficiency), this study demonstrates that machine learning can overcome this challenge. Specifically, the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm is applied to analyze complex health data metrics, simultaneously enhancing both accuracy and efficiency by reducing the number of samples transmitted while maintaining accuracy. The algorithm's performance is evaluated using a standard heart rate dataset, comparing its...

With 5G and the escalating demand for higher throughput, improving the spectral efficiency of wireless systems is paramount. In cognitive radio, significant throughput gains can be achieved if secondary users intelligently select *when* and *how often* to sense channels. We propose an algorithm that not only chooses a channel for data transmission but also predicts its unoccupied duration, thereby minimizing sensing time. Our two-stage learning process employs reinforcement learning for channel selection and a Bayesian approach to determine optimal sensing skip duration. Extensive simulations compare our method to other learning approaches. Results demonstrate minimized sensing with negligible primary interference, leading to reduced energy consumption for the secondary user and increased throughput by saving on sensing.

This paper examines model-free reinforcement learning for infinite-horizon discounted Markov Decision Processes (MDPs). We focus on scenarios with continuous state spaces and unknown transition kernels, where only a single sample path, generated by an arbitrary policy, is available.

We propose the Nearest Neighbor Q-Learning (NNQL) algorithm, which leverages nearest neighbor regression to learn the optimal Q-function. Our primary contribution is a rigorous finite-sample analysis of its convergence rate.

Specifically, for MDPs with a $d$-dimensional state space and a discount factor $\gamma \in (0,1)$, given a sample path with "covering time" $L$, we prove that NNQL can produce an $\varepsilon$-accurate estimate of the optimal Q-function using $\tilde{O}\big(L/(\varepsilon^3(1-\gamma)^7)\big)$ samples.

For example, in a well-behaved MDP, the covering time of a sample path generated by a purely random policy scales as $\tilde{O}\big(1/\varepsilon^d\big)$. In such cases, our analysis shows the sample complexity scales as $\tilde{O}\big(1/\varepsilon^{d+3}\big)$. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound of $\tilde{\Omega}\big(1/\varepsilon^{d+2}\big)$, demonstrating that our derived dependency is nearly optimal.

Despite progress in graph neural networks (GNNs) for graph data, training them on large datasets is challenging due to overfitting. While adversarial training, which uses worst-case adversarial examples to augment data, has been shown to improve model robustness and generalization against attacks, its impact on GNN generalization in graph analytics is not fully understood, as prior work primarily focused on defending against malicious attacks.

This paper examines GNNs through the lens of weight and feature loss landscapes, analyzing how loss changes with respect to model weights and node features. We find that GNNs tend to converge to sharp local minima in these landscapes, resulting in poor generalization. To address this, we propose a co-adversarial perturbation (CAP) optimization problem involving both weights and features, and develop an alternating adversarial perturbation algorithm to flatten these loss landscapes. Additionally, we introduce a two-stage training process: the first stage uses standard cross-entropy minimization for quick GNN convergence, and the second applies our alternating adversarial method.

UMAP has emerged as the preferred method for visualizing high-dimensional datasets across various fields, largely replacing t-SNE. However, the underlying reasons for its superior performance remain unclear. This work delves into UMAP's sampling-based optimization. We derive UMAP's true loss function and demonstrate its divergence from the previously published version. Consequently, UMAP does not, in fact, aim to accurately reflect its theoretically defined high-dimensional similarities. Instead, it seems to reproduce similarities primarily based on the shared k-nearest neighbor graph, challenging current assumptions about its efficacy. We propose that UMAP's success stems from its implicit balancing of attractive and repulsive forces through negative sampling, which in turn facilitates effective optimization via gradient descent. We validate our theoretical insights using both synthetic and single-cell RNA sequencing data.

Deep learning is advancing at an unprecedented pace, yielding a wide array of rapidly evolving models. This progress, however, comes with a significantly increasing demand for computational resources. Current deep learning frameworks, by optimizing for common network architectures, inadvertently limit the exploration and development of novel models crucial for research breakthroughs.

We address this limitation by introducing a flexible, user-customizable pipeline designed to optimize the training of diverse deep neural networks. Our approach prioritizes minimizing data movement throughout the training process. Starting with standard networks from PyTorch or ONNX, our pipeline progressively transforms computations through a series of lowering steps.

We have defined four distinct levels of general-purpose transformations, ranging from localized intra-operator optimizations to global data movement reduction. These transformations operate on a data-centric graph intermediate representation, which comprehensively captures both computation and data movement across various levels of abstraction. This includes expanding fundamental operators like convolutions into their underlying computational components.

A core principle of our design is its interactive and introspectable nature. The entire pipeline is extensible via a Python API, and users can interactively fine-tune parameters using a graphical user interface. We demonstrate the efficacy of our system by achieving competitive performance or significant speedups across ten different networks, notably uncovering new optimization opportunities in EfficientNet through interactive exploration.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) must be invariant to permutations of the adjacency matrix, a property known as graph isomorphism. Typically, this is achieved by using permutation-invariant operations during message aggregation. However, this approach can overlook relationships between neighboring nodes, limiting the GNNs' expressive power.

This work introduces an efficient permutation-sensitive aggregation mechanism utilizing permutation groups to capture pairwise correlations between neighboring nodes. We prove that our method surpasses the 2-dimensional Weisfeiler-Lehman (2-WL) graph isomorphism test in power and is at least as powerful as the 3-WL test. Additionally, our approach achieves linear sampling complexity. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our model.

This paper introduces CDML, a novel collaborative distillation meta-learning framework, to address simulation-intensive hardware design challenges. While deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has shown promise in hardware design, previous applications have been limited to problems with oversimplified objectives, lacking real-world practicality. The significant time and computational cost associated with evaluating real-world electrical performance through simulation renders DRL schemes, which rely on extensive reward calculations, unsuitable.

We apply the CDML framework to the decoupling capacitor placement problem (DPP), a prime example of a simulation-intensive hardware design problem. CDML comprises a context-based meta-learner and a collaborative distillation scheme, working together to produce a reusable solver. The context-based meta-learner enhances generalization by capturing the location of the probing port (i.e., the target circuit block). The collaborative distillation scheme, combined with equivariant label transformation, enforces the action-permutation (AP)-equivariant nature inherent in placement problems. This not only boosts sample efficiency but also improves generalization.

Extensive experimental results demonstrate that CDML surpasses both neural baselines and conventional iterative design methods in terms of real-world objectives, specifically power integrity, and exhibits zero-shot transferability.

Nonnegative Matrix Factorization (NMF) is a well-regarded technique for data analysis, yet its practical application faces increasing challenges due to the growing scale of modern datasets. To overcome this, we introduce a novel approach that leverages structured random compression—specifically, data-structure-aware random projections—for two NMF variations: classical NMF and separable NMF (SNMF).

For SNMF, where the left factors are a subset of the input matrix's columns, we develop tailored formulations. Our method accelerates existing algorithms, drastically cuts memory usage, and maintains performance comparable to uncompressed techniques. Furthermore, our structured random projections enable SNMF to efficiently process arbitrarily large matrices, moving beyond the typical tall-and-skinny constraint and significantly broadening its applicability.

We support our algorithmic innovations with theoretical underpinnings and diverse examples, demonstrating the effectiveness of our proposed methods.

This paper addresses counterfactual inference in sequentially designed experiments. We study the challenge of estimating outcomes under alternative policies when N units undergo T periods of intervention, and policies adapt over time. The inherent difficulty lies in the heterogeneity of outcomes across units and time.

To overcome this, we propose a latent factor model where potential outcomes are shaped by exogenous unit and time-level latent factors. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, missing potential outcomes can be estimated using a variation of nearest neighbors.

Our contributions are twofold:

1.  Assuming a bilinear latent factor model and an arbitrary adaptive sampling policy, we provide a distribution-free, non-asymptotic guarantee for estimating any missing outcome for any unit at any time. With suitable regularity, this guarantee implies consistency.
2.  For a general non-parametric latent factor model, we show that the estimate for any unit's missing outcome at time T satisfies a central limit theorem as T approaches infinity, given appropriate regularity conditions.

These findings allow us to establish...

Recent machine learning research has addressed increasingly large inputs, with cybersecurity, specifically sequence classification, posing particularly challenging long-sequence problems. For instance, detecting malware in Windows executables can involve inputs over 100 MB, equivalent to a time series of 100 million steps. Currently, MalConv, a convolutional neural network, is the closest solution, processing up to 2 million steps. However, the $\mathcal{O}(T)$ memory complexity of CNNs has limited their further application in malware analysis.

This work introduces a novel temporal max pooling method, decoupling memory requirements from sequence length $T$. This enhancement boosts MalConv's memory efficiency by 116x and accelerates training on its original dataset by up to 25.8x, while eliminating input length constraints. We leveraged these improvements to refine MalConv's architecture with a new Global Channel Gating design. This provides an attention mechanism that efficiently learns feature interactions across 100 million time steps, a capability absent in the original MalConv CNN. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/NeuromorphicComputationResearchProgram/MalConv2.

Malicious actors are increasingly leveraging botnets, posing a growing threat to numerous internet users. To combat this escalating danger, our research focuses on developing advanced botnet detection methods. We specifically target those elusive botnets that evade traditional detection techniques, such as signature-based and existing anomaly-based approaches.

Our core contribution is a novel machine learning method called Recurrent Variational Autoencoder (RVAE). RVAE is designed to detect botnets by analyzing the sequential characteristics of network traffic flow data. We demonstrate the robustness of RVAE using the CTU-13 dataset, intentionally configuring our testing dataset to include botnet types distinct from those used in training. Our evaluations confirm that RVAE achieves detection accuracy comparable to the leading results in existing literature.

Furthermore, we introduce an anomaly scoring approach based on probability distributions. This innovation enables real-time botnet detection in streaming mode, as new network statistics become available. This on-line detection capability is crucial for identifying previously unknown botnets in real-time.

Federated learning allows machine learning models to learn from decentralized private data while maintaining privacy. Typically, federated learning produces a single shared model for all participants. However, due to statistical heterogeneity and non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data across devices, this global model may perform worse for some clients than models trained solely on their local data. This reduces their incentive to participate. To address this, various personalization techniques have been developed to adapt global models for individual clients. This paper emphasizes the importance of such personalization and reviews recent research in this area.

This paper provides a tutorial and survey of Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, first- and second-order numerical optimization, and distributed optimization. We begin with a concise historical overview of optimization, followed by foundational concepts related to sets, norms, functions, and general optimization principles.

The paper then introduces the optimization problem, detailing standard problem types such as linear, quadratic, and semidefinite programming, as well as convex problems. We also explore techniques for handling constraints, including elimination methods, slack variables, and epigraph form.

A significant portion is dedicated to the Lagrangian function, dual variables, and the KKT conditions, encompassing primal and dual feasibility, weak and strong duality, complementary slackness, and the stationarity condition. We illustrate how these concepts are used to solve optimization problems via the method of Lagrange multipliers.

Next, we delve into first-order optimization methods, covering gradient descent, line-search techniques, convergence analysis of gradient methods, momentum, steepest descent, and backpropagation. Further first-order methods discussed include accelerated gradient methods, stochastic gradient descent (SGD), mini-batch SGD, stochastic average gradient (SAG), stochastic variance reduced gradient (SVRG), AdaGrad, RMSProp, and the Adam optimizer. The section also examines proximal methods, such as proximal mapping, the proximal point algorithm, and the proximal gradient method, alongside constrained gradient methods like the projected gradient method, projection onto convex sets, and the Frank-Wolfe method.

Finally, we address non-smooth and $\ell_1$ optimization techniques, exemplified by lasso regularization, the convex conjugate, the Huber function, and soft-thresholding.

Value function estimation, a crucial aspect of reinforcement learning, is essentially a prediction problem. While the Boltzmann softmax operator offers a natural and beneficial approach to value estimation, its lack of non-expansion property can lead to convergence failures, even in value iteration.

This paper introduces the Dynamic Boltzmann Softmax (DBS) operator, designed to update the value function with improved convergence properties in both planning and learning contexts. Our experiments in GridWorld demonstrate that the DBS operator enhances value function estimation, effectively resolving the convergence issues associated with the standard softmax operator.

Furthermore, we propose DBS-DQN, an algorithm that integrates dynamic Boltzmann softmax updates into deep Q-networks. DBS-DQN significantly outperforms standard DQN, achieving superior results in 40 out of 49 Atari games.

Bilevel optimization is a prevalent technique in machine learning, utilized in areas like hyperparameter tuning, policy optimization, and meta-learning. Despite recent advances in solving bilevel problems, existing methods often incur high computational costs and neglect generalized bilevel problems involving nonsmooth regularization. This paper introduces a novel suite of enhanced bilevel optimization methods leveraging Bregman distance. Our approach addresses bilevel problems where the outer subproblem can be nonconvex and potentially nonsmooth, while the inner subproblem is strongly convex.

Specifically, we present BiO-BreD (Bilevel Optimization based on Bregman Distance) for deterministic bilevel problems, demonstrating a computational complexity lower than state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we propose SBiO-BreD (Stochastic Bilevel Optimization based on Bregman Distance) for stochastic bilevel problems, which incorporates stochastic approximated gradients and Bregman distance. To further enhance performance, we introduce ASBiO-BreD, an accelerated version of SBiO-BreD that employs a variance-reduction technique. ASBiO-BreD achieves a superior computational complexity compared to existing methods for finding an $\epsilon$-stationary point, particularly concerning the condition number $\kappa$ and target accuracy $\epsilon$. We validate the superior performance of our algorithms against existing bilevel methods using a data hyper-cleaning task.

This paper outlines the methods and results from the DeeperForensics Challenge 2020, focusing on real-world face forgery detection. The challenge utilized the DeeperForensics-1.0 dataset, a comprehensive public resource for real-world face forgery detection, comprising 60,000 videos and 17.6 million frames. Model performance was evaluated online against a high-quality, hidden test set featuring diverse sources and distortions. The competition attracted 115 registered participants, with 25 teams submitting valid entries. This paper will summarize the winning approaches and discuss future research avenues.

Lifted Relational Neural Networks (LRNNs) employ weighted first-order rules to characterize relational domains, serving as blueprints for feed-forward neural networks. While LRNNs have achieved state-of-the-art results in various Inductive Logic Programming (ILP) tasks, their performance has historically relied on manually designed rules. This paper introduces an extension to the LRNN framework: structure learning, which fully automates the learning process. Similar to many ILP approaches, our structure learning algorithm iteratively explores the hypothesis space of Horn clauses through a top-down search. It considers predicates present in training data and generates "soft concepts" by inventing new predicates based on the most effective weighted rules discovered thus far. Our experiments demonstrate that this method can automatically induce beneficial hierarchical soft concepts, resulting in deep LRNNs with strong predictive capabilities.

Graph neural networks operate by converting the features of each vertex's neighborhood into a vector representation, which is then used independently to predict the vertex's label. This common approach presumes that vertex labels are conditionally independent, given their neighborhood features. However, this is a significant assumption that we demonstrate to be largely false across numerous real-world graph datasets.

For regression tasks, this conditional independence assumption severely constrains predictive accuracy. This limitation is not unexpected, given that traditional graph-based semi-supervised learning methods, like label propagation, explicitly model correlations in predicted outcomes.

We propose an interpretable and efficient framework to address this issue. Our method enhances any graph neural network architecture by leveraging the correlation structure within regression residuals. Specifically, we model the joint distribution of residuals across vertices using a parameterized multivariate Gaussian. We estimate these parameters by maximizing the marginal likelihood of the observed labels.

Our framework significantly outperforms existing baselines and provides learned parameters that reveal the strength of correlation among connected vertices. Additionally, we have developed linear-time algorithms for low-variance, unbiased estimation of model parameters.

Education, a common good rather than a privilege, must be universally accessible with minimal barriers. This is particularly crucial for key technologies like Machine Learning (ML) and Data Science (DS). Open Educational Resources (OER) are vital for achieving greater educational equity. This paper identifies specific requirements for ML and DS OER, emphasizing the unique importance of publicly available source files, which we term Open Source Educational Resources (OSER). We discuss our vision for collaborative OSER development, outline associated challenges, and propose initial solutions. We then explore OSER's application in blended learning and share our experiences in university settings. Finally, we address broader challenges such as credit assignment and certification.

A desirable property of statistical models, identifiability ensures that, with enough data and computational power, true model parameters can be estimated with arbitrary precision. This paper investigates identifiability within representation learning, specifically in discovering optimal nonlinear data representations for downstream tasks. While deep neural networks, often used for representation functions, typically lack identifiability in parameter space due to their inherent overparameterization, we leverage recent advancements in nonlinear Independent Component Analysis (ICA) to demonstrate that a significant class of discriminative models are, in fact, identifiable in function space, up to a linear transformation. This functional-space identifiability has been observed in numerous state-of-the-art representation learning models across diverse domains, including text, images, and audio. We establish sufficient conditions for this linear identifiability and support our findings with empirical evidence from both simulated and real-world datasets.

Our novel family of reinforcement learning operators aims to mitigate the adverse effects of approximation and estimation errors, thereby enhancing robustness. We establish several theoretical results, demonstrating that these operators preserve optimality and widen the action gap on a sample path basis. Empirical evidence highlights the superior performance of our operators, significantly surpassing both the classical Bellman operator and other recently proposed methods.

Our method prunes a random forest (RF) for efficient, resource-constrained prediction. We begin by building an RF, then strategically prune it to balance feature cost and accuracy. This pruning is framed as a novel 0-1 integer program, featuring linear constraints that promote feature re-use. We demonstrate the total unimodularity of the constraint set, proving that the linear programming relaxation yields the optimal integer solution. Drawing on insights from combinatorial optimization, we developed an efficient, scalable primal-dual algorithm. Unlike traditional top-down approaches—which are often intractable and rely on heuristics to acquire features based on utility—our bottom-up method benefits from a well-initialized RF. Empirical results show our pruning algorithm outperforms current state-of-the-art resource-constrained algorithms.

Infectious disease control is a critical health priority due to the potential for widespread human infection, leading to epidemics or pandemics. Consequently, early detection of these diseases is paramount, driving extensive research into diagnostic models. This paper reviews recent machine learning (ML) algorithms applied to infectious disease diagnosis, drawing from articles published between 2015 and 2022 in Web of Science, ScienceDirect, PubMed, Springer, and IEEE databases. We identify the strengths and weaknesses of these ML models and propose recommendations for future research in this area. Our analysis reveals a prevalence of small datasets and limited use of real-time data in the reviewed literature. We conclude that the most effective ML technique is contingent upon the characteristics of the dataset and the specific diagnostic objective.

This paper addresses the goodness-of-fit problem, specifically distinguishing whether observed data originate from a pre-defined distribution or from a composite alternative, where this alternative is separated from the null in terms of total variation.

For discrete data, our focus is on goodness-of-fit testing when the null distribution may involve a growing or unbounded number of categories.

For continuous data, we investigate the testing of Lipschitz densities, including those with potentially unbounded support, particularly in the low-smoothness regime where the Lipschitz parameter is not assumed to be constant.

Our findings reveal a significant departure from existing results: the minimax rate and critical testing radius in these scenarios are strongly and precisely dependent on the specific null distribution being tested. This dependence underscores the importance of studying the local minimax rate as a function of the null distribution.

Building on the recent work of Valiant and Valiant on the local minimax rate for multinomials, we revisit and extend their findings. We also introduce and characterize the performance of two modified chi-squared tests.
