Bike-sharing is a growing component of urban transport, and precise demand prediction is crucial for efficient re-balancing and service delivery. Current prediction models typically rely solely on historical bike-sharing data, treating it as an isolated system and ignoring its interplay with other transport modes. This is a significant oversight, as bike-sharing often complements other travel options, such as public transit. While some progress has been made, no existing method effectively utilizes spatiotemporal information from multiple modes with diverse spatial units. To bridge this gap, this study introduces B-MRGNN, a graph-based deep learning approach for bike-sharing demand prediction that integrates multimodal historical data. It encodes spatial dependencies across modes using multiple intra- and inter-modal graphs. A multi-relational graph neural network (MRGNN) is employed to capture correlations between spatial units across modes, including bike-sharing stations, subway stations, and ride-hailing zones. Extensive experiments using real-world data from New York City's bike-sharing, subway, and ride-hailing systems demonstrate B-MRGNN's superior performance over current methods.

The Gaussian-smoothed optimal transport (GOT) framework, introduced by Goldfeld et al. (2020) and further developed in subsequent research, has rapidly become a focal point for researchers across statistics, machine learning, information theory, and related disciplines. A crucial insight from this work is that adopting the GOT framework, as opposed to its unsmoothed equivalent, mitigates the curse of dimensionality when using empirical measures to approximate true data-generating distributions.

This paper demonstrates a similar principle applies to estimating nonparametric mixing distributions within discrete exponential family models. Specifically, we show that using the GOT cost dramatically accelerates the estimation accuracy of the nonparametric Maximum Likelihood Estimator (MLE) to a polynomial rate. This stands in stark contrast to classical sub-polynomial rates derived from unsmoothed metrics, which are information-theoretically unimprovable. A pivotal element of our analysis is the derivation of a novel Jackson-type approximation bound for Gaussian-convoluted Lipschitz functions, which bridges existing methods for analyzing nonparametric MLEs with the innovative GOT framework.

Machine Learning (ML) has emerged as a significant and versatile tool for disease diagnosis, attracting substantial interest from both researchers and practitioners. Given the rapid progress in ML and the increasing volume of related publications, a thorough review of Machine Learning-Based Disease Diagnosis (MLBDD) is imperative. This article presents a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of MLBDD literature published between 2012 and 2021.

Using specific keywords, we extracted 1710 relevant papers and their associated data from the Scopus and Web of Science (WOS) databases. This information was then compiled into an Excel datasheet for subsequent analysis. Our study first investigates publication trends, identifying the most prolific countries/regions, institutions, and authors. Second, we visualize co-citation networks of countries/regions, institutions, authors, and articles using R-studio software. These networks are further analyzed to understand their citation structures and identify influential entities.

This research offers a valuable overview of MLBDD for those new to the field, while also providing a comprehensive foundation for researchers planning further investigations.

This paper presents a novel inference method for stochastic epidemic models. Our approach tackles the challenge of intractable likelihoods by employing recursive multinomial approximations to integrate out unobserved variables. It is suitable for discrete-time, finite-population compartmental models with partial, randomly under-reported, or missing count observations. Unlike conventional methods such as Approximate Bayesian Computation, our technique eliminates the need for forward model simulation and tuning parameters. The approximate marginal likelihood of model parameters is computed efficiently via a simple filtering recursion. We demonstrate the method's accuracy using both real and simulated data, including an analysis of the 1995 Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Furthermore, we illustrate its integration into a Sequential Monte Carlo framework for estimating the time-varying reproduction number of COVID-19, building on the work of Kucharski et al. (2020) on the Wuhan outbreak.

Machine Learning has recently experienced rapid growth, leading to its widespread adoption in various domains such as educational assessments, credit risk, healthcare, employment, and criminal justice. This increased integration necessitates ensuring the trustworthiness of ML and Natural Language Processing (NLP) systems, particularly regarding the fairness and robustness of their decisions. To address this, we introduce GYC, a framework designed to generate counterfactual text samples essential for rigorously testing these ML systems.

Our contributions are twofold:

a) We present GYC, a novel framework for generating counterfactual samples. This framework is designed to produce generations that are plausible, diverse, goal-oriented, and effective.

b) GYC can generate counterfactual samples that specifically target desired conditions, such as named-entity tags, semantic role labels, or sentiment.

Our experimental results across diverse domains demonstrate that GYC effectively generates counterfactual text samples exhibiting these four key properties. These GYC-generated counterfactuals serve as valuable test cases for evaluating both ML models and text debiasing algorithms.

Generating realistic, long-range human action sequences from skeletons is difficult because minor single-frame errors can deform an entire action. Current approaches, often adapted from video generation, often misrepresent skeleton nodes as simple pixels, overlooking crucial inter- and intra-frame structural details, which can result in distorted actions. While Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) offer a promising avenue for learning structural representations, directly applying them to the continuous spatial and temporal dimensions of action sequences is problematic due to the potentially massive action graphs involved. To address this, we introduce a novel GCN variant that employs a self-attention mechanism to adaptively sparsify the action graph in the temporal domain. Our method dynamically identifies and focuses on significant past frames, constructing a sparse graph that integrates seamlessly with the GCN framework, thereby effectively capturing the inherent structural information within action sequences. Our extensive experiments on two benchmark human action datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our method compared to existing techniques.

This paper introduces deep multimodal learning techniques for Audio-Visual Automatic Speech Recognition (AV-ASR), focusing on fusing speech and visual data.

Our first approach involves training separate unimodal deep networks. The final hidden layers of these networks are then fused to create a joint feature space, which serves as the input for an additional deep network. This fusion model achieved a Phone Error Rate (PER) of 35.83% on the IBM large vocabulary audio-visual studio dataset. This significantly improves upon the 41% PER of the audio-only network under clean conditions, highlighting the substantial contribution of the visual channel to phone classification, even when audio quality is high.

Secondly, we propose a novel deep network architecture featuring a bilinear softmax layer designed to capture class-specific correlations between modalities. Combining the posteriors from these bilinear networks with those from our initial fusion model further reduces the PER, achieving a final rate of 34.03%.

We introduce effective pre-training strategies for Neural Machine Translation (NMT) that leverage parallel corpora with a pivot language (source-pivot and pivot-target). These strategies significantly enhance source-target translation quality. We propose three methods to strengthen the interconnections between source, pivot, and target languages during pre-training: 1) a step-wise training approach for a single model across various language pairs, 2) the integration of an adapter component to seamlessly link pre-trained encoders and decoders, and 3) cross-lingual encoder training through pivot language autoencoding. Our methods demonstrably outperform multilingual models, achieving gains of up to +2.6% BLEU in the WMT 2019 French-German and German-Czech tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate the efficacy of our improvements in zero-shot/zero-resource environments.

Event generators are crucial tools in high-energy nuclear and particle physics for studying particle reactions. This paper surveys the current landscape of machine learning (ML) applications in developing these generators. We review the ML generative models employed in ML-based event generators, highlighting their unique challenges. Furthermore, we discuss various strategies for integrating physics principles into ML model designs to address these difficulties. Finally, we explore open questions concerning super-resolution, fidelity, and extrapolation in the context of ML-driven physics event generation.

This study explores methods for detecting imagined speech segments from continuous electroencephalogram (EEG) signals, a crucial step for developing asynchronous Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs). Such BCIs empower users to control external devices or communicate messages at will by decoding their imagined speech. We present five feature extraction techniques—based on wavelet decomposition, empirical mode decomposition, frequency energies, fractal dimension, and chaos theory—to identify the onset of imagined words within a continuous EEG stream. These methods were evaluated across three datasets using four distinct classifiers, achieving F1 scores of 0.73, 0.79, and 0.68. These promising results suggest the feasibility of automating imagined word segmentation for subsequent BCI classification.

Pixelated Platonic solids, like cubes and icosahedra, are commonly used to represent spherical data, from climate patterns to Cosmic Microwave Background radiation. These solids possess inherent global symmetries. When their faces are pixelated, each face also exhibits local symmetries through Euclidean isometries. Current methods of combining these symmetries, often hierarchical, fail to fully capture their interaction. We propose a group theory-inspired framework to model this interplay, identifying equivariant linear maps and introducing symmetry-preserving equivariant padding. Deep networks built with these tools generalize gauge-equivariant CNNs on pixelated spheres, achieving state-of-the-art results in climate data semantic segmentation and omnidirectional image processing. Code is available at https://git.io/JGiZA.

Commonsense reasoning systems ideally generalize across diverse scenarios. However, current top methods often rely on costly data and overspecialize in benchmarks, failing to acquire broad semantic reasoning skills. Zero-shot QA systems offer a promising alternative, transforming commonsense knowledge graphs (KGs) into synthetic training data. Given the proliferation of KGs, this paper proposes a multi-source zero-shot transfer learning approach, synergistically leveraging multiple KGs. To address potential knowledge interference, we introduce a modular knowledge aggregation method as a novel zero-shot commonsense reasoning framework. Our framework demonstrably enhances performance across five commonsense benchmarks, effectively utilizing multiple KGs.

This paper introduces Lattice Cross Fusion, a novel strategy for integrating multistream convolutional networks. This method fuses signals from convolutional layers through mathematical operations applied just before pooling layers. When tested on a modified AlexNet-LCNN version using a deliberately degraded CIFAR-10 dataset, this new approach demonstrated superior performance, outperforming the baseline single-stream network by 46% with improved convergence speed, stability, and robustness.

Predicting and understanding chemical reactions are crucial for studying complex chemical systems. Reactive molecular dynamics (MD) simulations are a valuable tool for this purpose, providing atomic-level insights that aid in interpreting reaction mechanisms. In this research, we developed two reference datasets and trained corresponding neural network (NN) potentials. These NN potentials can predict potential energy and atomic forces with DFT accuracy for large-scale reaction systems, but at significantly faster speeds than traditional DFT calculations. We then used these models to conduct reactive MD simulations, investigating the combustion mechanisms of hydrogen and methane. The efficiency of the NN model allowed us to generate nanosecond MD trajectories for large systems (hundreds of atoms) and uncover detailed combustion mechanisms. The algorithms developed in this study have the potential to explore and discover reaction mechanisms in a wide range of complex systems, including combustion, synthesis, and heterogeneous catalysis, without requiring predefined reaction coordinates or elementary reaction steps.

Given the inherent opacity of deep learning models, explainable AI methods are vital for fostering human trust and facilitating AI-human collaboration. This paper explores various model-agnostic and CNN-specific explanation techniques for text classification. We conduct three human-centric evaluations, each designed to assess a distinct purpose of explanations: (1) illuminating model behavior, (2) justifying model predictions, and (3) aiding human investigation of uncertain predictions. Our findings reveal significant differences in the quality of the explanation methods examined and demonstrate their varying effectiveness across these three purposes.

The past decade saw an explosion in data volumes and computational complexity across many fields, necessitating highly data-parallel computing within distributed systems. Managing these systems efficiently is difficult due to unpredictable job and task performance under different resource configurations, which impacts scheduling and resource allocation. This survey explores predictive performance modeling (PPM) techniques that estimate future job and task performance metrics—like execution time, memory usage, or wait times—by analyzing past observations. We focus on non-intrusive methods, applicable to any workload without modification, given that workloads are typically black boxes to the systems managing the computational infrastructure. We categorize and compare factors contributing to performance variation, predicted metrics, necessary training data, use cases, and the underlying prediction methodologies. Finally, we identify key open problems and urgent research needs in this domain.

Autonomous systems often impact multiple users simultaneously, making fairness in their design paramount. This paper addresses the challenge of training reinforcement learning (RL) agents to achieve equitable treatment of users, a departure from conventional RL approaches. We define a novel RL problem centered on optimizing a formally defined fairness objective function. We provide a theoretical analysis of this problem, considering both discounted and average reward settings. Our analysis yields a new result applicable to standard RL: a novel bound on the approximation error between the optimal average reward and the average reward achieved by a policy optimized for discounted rewards. This finding is significant because learning with discounted rewards is typically simpler, thereby validating the strategy of deriving fair policies for average rewards from policies optimized for discounted rewards. We then detail how established deep RL algorithms can be adapted to our fair optimization framework and present extensive experimental validation across three distinct domains.

The growing prevalence of network datasets—encompassing social, biological, and information networks—has underscored the significance of relational data representations. This, in turn, has fueled the application of statistical relational learning (SRL) algorithms in these domains. This article delves into various representation challenges inherent in graph-based relational data. Given that the choice of how to represent nodes, links, and features profoundly impacts SRL algorithm performance, we explore methods and possibilities for transforming relational representations to enhance these algorithms.

To that end, we present a straightforward taxonomy for data representation transformations in relational domains, treating link and node transformations as symmetrical tasks. Specifically, for both nodes and links, transformation tasks include: (i) predicting their existence, (ii) predicting their label or type, (iii) estimating their weight or importance, and (iv) systematically constructing their relevant features. We illustrate our taxonomy with detailed examples, using it to survey and compare different approaches for each task. We also discuss general conditions for transforming links, nodes, and features. Finally, we identify remaining challenges.

Bayesian nonparametric (BNP) models excel at uncovering latent features in data, yet their inference can be computationally intensive. We leverage the decomposable nature of completely random measures—the foundation for popular models like the Dirichlet process and beta-Bernoulli process—into independent sub-measures. This allows us to partition the latent measure into two parts: a finite measure comprising instantiated components and an infinite measure containing all others. We then apply distinct inference algorithms to each: uncollapsed samplers for the finite measure, and collapsed samplers for the sparse, infinite tail. This hybrid approach, applicable to a broad range of models, is easily parallelizable, enabling scalable inference while preserving asymptotic convergence guarantees.

We investigate the cross-entropy method (CEM) for non-convex optimization of continuous, parameterized objective functions. We propose a differentiable variant that allows for differentiation of CEM's output with respect to the objective function's parameters. This innovation integrates CEM into end-to-end machine learning pipelines, a previously unachievable feat. We demonstrate its utility in a synthetic energy-based structured prediction task and in non-convex continuous control. For control, we illustrate how to embed optimal action sequences into a lower-dimensional space. Our differentiable CEM (DCEM) also enables fine-tuning of CEM-based controllers through policy optimization.

This paper introduces an efficient variational inference framework for developing Structured Gaussian Process Regression Network (SGPRN) models. Our core innovation involves integrating auxiliary inducing variables into latent functions and simultaneously treating the distributions of both inducing variables and hyperparameters as variational parameters. We then propose structured variable distributions and marginalize latent variables, which facilitates the decomposition of a tractable variational lower bound and enables stochastic optimization. This inference approach allows us to model data where outputs may not share a common input set, with a computational complexity independent of input and output sizes, making it well-suited for handling datasets with missing values. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on synthetic and real datasets, showing that our model generally outperforms state-of-the-art methods in imputing missing data. Furthermore, we present a visualization technique for time-varying correlations across outputs in electrocorticography data, offering valuable insights into neural population dynamics.

Extracting structured information as a knowledge graph from literary texts like novels or short stories presents a challenge due to the vast number of potential relationships between characters and the difficulty in obtaining supervised data for them. Our approach tackles this as an unsupervised task, leveraging transformers. We embed relational sentences from the text using SBERT and then cluster them to group semantically similar relationships. Sentences within each cluster are then summarized with BART, and a descriptive label is extracted from the summary. Initial results indicate that this clustering effectively identifies similar relationships, offering a valuable preprocessing step for semi-supervised methods.

Manifold learning employs dimensionality reduction to identify a projection subspace that selectively amplifies inter-class variance while diminishing intra-class variance. However, the efficacy of current subspace learning methods is often hampered by the high dimensionality of datasets. This paper introduces a hierarchical approach designed to enhance the scalability of subspace learning methods, aiming to improve classification accuracy in large datasets by 3% to 10%. We explore various methodological combinations and evaluate our proposed approach on five publicly available large datasets. Our analysis incorporates several eigenvalue-based subspace learning techniques, including linear discriminant analysis, principal component analysis, generalized discriminant analysis, and reconstruction independent component analysis. To further assess its impact, the output of our method is fed into diverse classification algorithms such as linear discriminant analysis, quadratic linear analysis, k-nearest neighbor, and random forest classifiers. A comparative analysis of the resulting classification accuracies demonstrates the effectiveness of our hierarchical approach, yielding an average increase of 5% in classification accuracy.

Recent advancements in deep learning have dramatically improved brain tumor segmentation. Yet, fully supervised training demands extensive, expertly annotated masks, a process that is both time-consuming and resource-intensive. Weakly supervised learning, particularly with scribbles, offers a compelling balance between model accuracy and labeling effort. However, segmenting the hierarchical structures of brain tumors still presents a challenge, as manually labeling scribbles for each substructure remains demanding.

This paper introduces a novel deep learning approach that leverages only two types of weak labels: scribbles delineating the whole tumor and healthy brain tissue, and global labels indicating the presence of each substructure. Our method segments all sub-regions through a two-phase training process involving two networks. Initially, we train a whole tumor (WT) segmentation network using only whole tumor scribbles, which provides an approximate WT mask for the training data. Subsequently, we cluster the WT region, guided by global labels. The resulting preliminary substructure segmentations from this clustering serve as weak labels for training the second network. We further refine this weakly supervised segmentation using a dense Conditional Random Field (CRF) loss.

Evaluated on the BraTS2017 dataset, our approach achieves competitive Dice scores for whole tumor segmentation and comparable scores for individual substructures.

This work investigates adversarial attacks on Variational Autoencoders (VAEs). We demonstrate methods for manipulating data points to achieve either a specific latent code (supervised attack) or a significantly altered one (unsupervised attack). We further analyze how model variations, such as $\beta$-VAE and NVAE, impact VAE robustness and propose metrics for its quantification.

The SLOPE estimator, a recent innovation (arXiv:1407.3824), has demonstrated adaptive achievement of the minimax $\ell_2$ estimation rate in high-dimensional sparse linear regression, particularly when sparsity ($k$), sample size ($n$), and dimension ($p$) adhere to $k/p \rightarrow 0$ and $k\log p/n \rightarrow 0$ (arXiv:1503.08393). This paper investigates SLOPE's estimation error in a different regime, where $k$ and $n$ scale linearly with $p$, offering fresh insights into its performance. We begin by deriving a concentration inequality for SLOPE's finite sample mean square error (MSE). While the MSE's central value is complex and implicit, our analysis reveals that LASSO is the optimal SLOPE estimator for $k$-sparse parameter vectors without tied non-zero components, given low noise. Conversely, under high noise, SLOPE estimators, including LASSO, are suboptimal compared to bridge regression methods like Ridge.

This paper contributes two key advancements. First, we introduce mixed compositional kernels and mixed Neural Network Gaussian Processes (NGGPs). Mixed compositional kernels are formed by composing probability generating functions (PGFs). A mixed NNGP is a Gaussian process (GP) utilizing such a kernel, emerging as the infinite-width limit of multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) where each layer employs a distinct activation function. Second, we present $\theta$ activation functions for neural networks and $\theta$ compositional kernels, drawing upon the theory of branching processes, specifically $\theta$ PGFs. Notably, while $\theta$ compositional kernels are recursive, they possess a closed-form expression. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, $\theta$ compositional kernels exhibit non-degenerate asymptotic properties. This implies that GPs employing $\theta$ compositional kernels avoid the need for non-explicit recursive kernel evaluations and offer controllable infinite-depth asymptotic behaviors. A remaining open question is whether GPs with $\theta$ compositional kernels represent the limits of infinitely-wide MLPs equipped with $\theta$ activation functions.

Early diagnosis of sacroiliitis is crucial for initiating preventive treatment and significantly improving patients' long-term quality of life. While CT scans of the lower back or abdomen are commonly performed for suspected back pain, subtle early-stage differences between healthy and inflamed sacroiliac joints can lead to missed diagnoses.

We have developed a novel automatic algorithm for the incidental diagnosis and grading of sacroiliitis from CT scans of patients undergoing evaluation for lower back pain. This method leverages supervised machine and deep learning techniques. The algorithm takes a CT scan containing the patient's pelvis as input and outputs a diagnosis for each sacroiliac joint.

The algorithm proceeds in four steps:
1.  **Initial Region of Interest (ROI) Computation:** An initial ROI encompassing the pelvic joints is identified using heuristics and a U-Net classifier.
2.  **ROI Refinement:** The ROI is further refined to precisely locate both sacroiliac joints using a four-tree random forest.
3.  **Individual Sacroiliitis Grading (Slice-wise):** Each sacroiliac joint in every CT slice is individually graded for sacroiliitis using a custom slice CNN classifier.
4.  **Overall Diagnosis and Grading:** Sacroiliitis diagnosis and overall grading are determined by combining the individual slice grades using a random forest.

Automated medical image segmentation is difficult because it needs a lot of hand-labeled data. However, current learning methods often struggle with limited annotated data, which hurts accuracy. Existing semi-supervised methods are often less robust than supervised ones and don't explicitly model geometric or semantic information, limiting their precision.

We introduce SimCVD, a straightforward contrastive distillation framework that significantly improves voxel-wise representation learning. Our unsupervised training strategy uses two views of an input volume to predict signed distance maps of object boundaries through a contrastive objective, using only two independent dropout masks. This simple method performs surprisingly well, matching fully supervised methods with far less labeled data. We believe dropout acts as a minimal data augmentation, preventing representation collapse.

We also propose structural distillation by leveraging pairwise similarities. We tested SimCVD on the Left Atrial Segmentation Challenge (LA) dataset and another.

Introducing the Convolutional Conditional Neural Process (ConvCNP), a novel addition to the Neural Process family. This model incorporates translation equivariance, a crucial inductive bias for diverse learning tasks such as time series analysis, spatial data processing, and image understanding. Unlike traditional approaches that embed datasets into finite-dimensional vector spaces, the ConvCNP maps them into an infinite-dimensional function space. To formalize this, we expand the theory of neural set representations to include functional representations, proving that any translation-equivariant embedding can be realized through a convolutional deep set. Our evaluations show that ConvCNPs outperform existing Neural Processes, achieving state-of-the-art results across various benchmarks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that integrating translation equivariance facilitates zero-shot generalization to complex, out-of-domain scenarios.

Max-cut, clustering, and other significant partitioning problems in machine learning and science are NP-hard. This has led to the development of numerous approximation algorithms and heuristics. While the optimal algorithm often depends on the specific application, comparing algorithms through worst-case analysis can be misleading if such instances are rare. Therefore, there's a need for optimization methods that identify the best algorithm configuration for an application's typical inputs.

We address this for clustering, max-cut, and other partitioning problems, including integer quadratic programming. We design computationally and sample-efficient learning algorithms that, given samples from an application-specific distribution of problem instances, learn a partitioning algorithm with high expected performance. Our algorithms learn across common integer quadratic programming and clustering algorithm families: SDP rounding algorithms and agglomerative clustering algorithms with dynamic programming.

For our sample complexity analysis, we provide tight bounds on the pseudodimension of these algorithm classes, revealing that even for algorithm classes parameterized by a single variable, the pseudodimension is superconstant. This work contributes to the foundations of this field.

Deep learning models have achieved remarkable empirical success, yet our understanding of the underlying reasons for this performance remains limited. To address this, we examine the decision boundary of a deep learning architecture in production, making minimal assumptions about both the training data and the model.

We demonstrate, theoretically and empirically, that the final weight layer of a neural network converges to a linear Support Vector Machine (SVM). This holds true for both binary and multi-class classification, particularly when using the common cross-entropy loss and training on the output of the penultimate hidden layer.

Furthermore, our empirical findings suggest that end-to-end neural network training, as opposed to merely fine-tuning the last weight layer, can lead to a more favorable bias constant for that layer, which is crucial for generalization.

Beyond enhancing our comprehension of deep learning, these results offer insights that could aid in tackling various practical challenges, including catastrophic forgetting and adversarial attacks.

The code for our experiments is available at: https://github.com/lykaust15/NN_decision_boundary

End-to-end learning frameworks are increasingly common in robot control, directly mapping states or images to torque or action parameters. However, their substantial data demands for task learning raise concerns about scalability across multiple tasks, as training often necessitates hundreds or thousands of examples. This prompts the question: must end-to-end approaches learn a unique model for each task? Intuitively, sharing knowledge across tasks seems beneficial, given that all tasks require a fundamental understanding of the environment. This paper explores a progression in data-driven end-to-end learning: transitioning from task-specific models to jointly learning multiple robot tasks. Remarkably, our findings indicate that multi-task learning models outperform task-specific models trained with equivalent data. For instance, a deep network trained with 2,500 grasp and 2,500 push examples exhibits superior grasping performance compared to a network trained solely on 5,000 grasp examples.

In this paper, we explore the relationship between Shannon's channels, formed by transition probability functions, and semantic channels, constructed from truth functions. We define label learning as the process of aligning semantic channels with Shannon's channels, and label selection as the inverse. The multi-label classification problem is addressed by the Channel Matching (CM) algorithm, which operates under the principle of maximum semantic information—a principle consistent with both maximum likelihood and regularized least squares criteria.

For large datasets, Shannon's channels can be directly transformed into semantic channels using a third type of Bayes' theorem. For smaller datasets, we can train parameterized truth functions using sampling distributions. We consider labels that may be Boolean functions of atomic labels; however, for simplified learning, we may focus on obtaining truth functions for only the atomic labels.

To avoid issues associated with binary relevance, we categorize instances into three types—positive, negative, and unclear—rather than the conventional two. For each instance, the classifier identifies a compound label that conveys the most semantic information or exhibits the richest connotation. Importantly, as a predictive model, the semantic channel remains unaffected by the prior probability distribution of instances, ensuring its continued efficacy even when the source distribution changes.

Interactive reinforcement learning agents can benefit from human feedback, especially in complex environments. Traditionally, this feedback is a simple positive or negative signal. However, such discrete signals can be challenging for agents to generalize effectively.

This paper proposes using natural language advice to provide richer feedback to reinforcement learning agents. We extend policy shaping, a common interactive reinforcement learning technique, by replacing its traditional human feedback policy with one generated from natural language advice. Our goal is to determine if natural language reasoning can help deep reinforcement learning agents make better decisions.

Our model incorporates three distinct networks: an experience-driven network, an advice generator, and an advice-driven network. The experience-driven reinforcement learning agent selects actions based on environmental rewards. In contrast, the advice-driven neural network leverages feedback generated by the advice generator for new situations.

We introduce an algorithm that merges the computational efficiency of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with the second-order curvature information characteristic of quasi-Newton methods for minimizing sums of functions. Our approach unifies these distinct methodologies by assigning a separate Hessian approximation to each individual function within the sum. To manage computational demands and memory footprint, particularly in high-dimensional optimization, we store and manipulate these quadratic approximations within a shared, evolving, low-dimensional subspace. Similar to SGD, each update step necessitates evaluating only a single contributing function or minibatch. Furthermore, like quasi-Newton methods, each step is scaled using an approximate inverse Hessian, largely eliminating the need for hyperparameter tuning. This method diverges from prior stochastic second-order techniques that often treat individual function Hessians as noisy estimates of the overall Hessian; instead, our algorithm directly estimates them. Experimental results across seven diverse optimization problems demonstrate improved convergence. The algorithm is openly available as Python and MATLAB packages.

This paper introduces a novel learning algorithm for probabilistic spiking neural networks (SNNs). Building on the stochastic variational inference framework by Jimenez Rezende & Gerstner (2014) for SNNs with hidden neurons, we address a key limitation: the high variance of the score function gradient estimator, which often hinders learning. Our solution is an alternative gradient estimator for SNNs, derived using the path-wise gradient method.

A significant challenge in applying the path-wise method is the absence of a general technique for differentiating a realization of an arbitrary point process, a prerequisite for this estimator. Our primary technical contribution is the development of a differentiable point process, which enables us to derive the path-wise gradient estimator for SNNs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this new estimator through numerical simulations.

Traditional clustering methods often rely on analyzing feature spaces. However, many real-world datasets include spatial information and inherently spatially coherent classes. Standard clustering techniques may not adequately capture this spatial coherence. To address this, particularly in hyperspectral imaging, we propose novel clustering models. These models utilize orthogonal nonnegative matrix factorization and incorporate total variation (TV) regularization on the cluster membership matrix to ensure spatial coherence. We explore various optimization strategies, applying TV regularization either as a post-processing step or directly integrating it into the clustering algorithm. Our numerical evaluation on a hyperspectral dataset, obtained from a matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization imaging measurement, demonstrates that our proposed methods yield significantly improved clustering results compared to conventional approaches.

We introduce DMV, a new memory-based tracker that leverages part-level dense memory and voting-based retrieval. While Siamese trackers have gained popularity in deep learning-based tracking for their speed-accuracy balance, their reliance on single template matching limits performance by restricting information to initial target features. Our method overcomes this limitation by maintaining an external memory of tracking records. Part-level retrieval from this memory disentangles information from the template, enabling our tracker to better handle appearance changes and occlusions. Memory updates during tracking enhance the target object's representational power without online learning. Additionally, we propose a novel voting mechanism for memory reading to filter unreliable information. Comprehensive evaluations on OTB-100, TrackingNet, GOT-10k, LaSOT, and UAV123 demonstrate that DMV achieves state-of-the-art comparable results.

Given the widespread use and importance of online payment systems, detecting fraudulent transactions is crucial for ensuring user account safety and platform security. This paper introduces a novel method for fraud detection that integrates patterns from both static user profiles and dynamic user behaviors within a unified framework. To effectively process continuous-time user behavior data, we propose using *time attention-based recurrent layers*. These layers embed detailed temporal information—such as action durations, time differences between actions, and sequential behavior patterns—into a shared latent space. We then combine these learned embeddings with static user profiles within a cohesive framework. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across various evaluation metrics, particularly *recall at top percent*, an important measure for balancing user experience and potential financial risk.

This paper qualitatively compares evolutionary strategies and reinforcement learning, specifically the OpenAI-ES and PPO algorithms—chosen for their methodological similarities. We investigate differences across five key areas: general efficacy, handling sparse rewards, ability to find minimal solutions, reliance on reward shaping, and adaptability to environmental changes. Our analysis, based on performance and behavioral strategies in benchmark problems, reveals novel qualitative distinctions, identifies each method's weaknesses, and suggests improvements. We further demonstrate that reward function characteristics significantly impact performance not only for OpenAI-ES and PPO but also for other reinforcement learning algorithms, highlighting the critical need to tailor reward functions to specific algorithms.

Adversarial Training (AT) and Virtual Adversarial Training (VAT) are regularization techniques that enhance Deep Neural Network (DNN) robustness by training them with adversarial examples. These examples are created by applying small, carefully chosen "worst-case" additive perturbations to input data. This paper introduces xAT and xVAT, novel adversarial training algorithms that instead generate **multiplicative** perturbations for robust DNN training.

These multiplicative perturbations possess distinct advantages over their additive counterparts used in traditional AT and VAT: they are significantly more perceptible and interpretable. Furthermore, while standard AT and VAT are limited to transductive implementation, our multiplicative perturbations can be generated either transductively or inductively.

Through extensive experimentation, we analyze the behavior of these multiplicative perturbations. Our results demonstrate that xAT and xVAT achieve classification accuracies comparable to or surpassing state-of-the-art methods across various established benchmarks. Notably, our methods are also approximately 30% faster than their additive counterparts. Additionally, the DNNs resulting from xAT and xVAT exhibit distinct weight distributions.

This paper bridges the gap between two established methods for handling unknown probabilities: Bayesian inference with a second-order prior and the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm for incomplete data. Specifically, we integrate these approaches for Dirichlet priors. We derive efficient approximations for the mean, mode, and (co)variance of both the probabilities and the mutual information. A key finding is the proof of unimodality for the posterior distribution, which guarantees that EM converges to the global maximum within this framework. We apply these results to feature selection for incremental learning and naive Bayes classification. Our novel filter, based on the distribution of mutual information, demonstrates superior performance over traditional empirical mutual information filters on various incomplete real-world datasets.

This paper presents a versatile set of convex fairness regularizers for linear and logistic regression, enabling efficient optimization. These regularizers encompass a spectrum of fairness concepts, from group-based to strong individual fairness. By adjusting the weight of the fairness regularizer, we can determine the optimal accuracy-fairness trade-off for any dataset. We quantify this trade-off using a metric called the Price of Fairness (PoF). A key contribution of our work is a comprehensive comparative analysis of the PoF across six diverse datasets where fairness is a critical concern.

Recent advancements in 3D object detection, particularly those leveraging point clouds, have been significant. However, much of this progress has focused on developing deep learning architectures primarily aimed at improving accuracy. This paper introduces an autoencoder-style framework designed for knowledge distillation, featuring channel-wise compression and decompression facilitated by interchange transfer.

To enable our student network to learn the teacher network's map-view features, we independently feed features from both networks through a shared autoencoder. Within this process, we employ a compressed representation loss that acts as a regularization, binding the channel-wise compressed knowledge from both networks. Subsequently, the decompressed features are exchanged in opposite directions to minimize discrepancies in the interchange reconstructions. Finally, we incorporate an attentive head loss to align the critical detection information derived from the multi-head self-attention mechanism.

Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that this method effectively trains lightweight models well-suited for 3D point cloud detection. We further validate its superior performance on the widely recognized Waymo and nuScenes public datasets.

This paper introduces an image classification dataset of executable code, comprising 10 distinct classes: 9 malicious virus families and one benign set. The dataset contains approximately 50,000 virus examples. The first 1024 bytes of each Portable Executable (PE) are formatted as images, akin to the MNIST handwriting dataset, enabling the application of existing algorithmic methods with minimal adjustments. The 9 virus families were identified through unsupervised learning, specifically KMeans clustering applied to the malicious examples. Using MobileNetV2, a deep learning model, we achieved an 80% overall accuracy in classifying virus families when including benignware. Furthermore, upon positive malware detection (via signature or heuristics), projecting the initial 1024 bytes into a thumbnail image allows for 87% accurate virus type classification. This research extends previous findings by demonstrating the effectiveness of convolutional neural networks—originally designed for image processing—in a novel abstract domain: pixel bytes derived from executable files. The dataset is accessible on Kaggle and GitHub.

Width-based planning has demonstrated impressive performance on Atari 2600 games, achieving strong results with pixel input and significantly fewer environment interactions compared to reinforcement learning. Prior width-based methods have relied on either hand-crafted features or VAEs trained on game screens (VAE-IW) to generate feature vectors for each screen, subsequently pruning screens that lack novel features during the search process. We introduce Olive (Online-VAE-IW), a novel approach that employs active learning to update VAE features online, thereby maximizing the utility of screens observed during planning. Our experiments across 55 Atari games show Olive outperforming Rollout-IW 42-to-11 and VAE-IW 32-to-20. Furthermore, Olive surpasses policy-learning methods like $\pi$-IW and DQN, even when these are trained with 100 times the budget (30-to-22 and 31-to-17 wins, respectively). Remarkably, Olive also outperforms EfficientZero, a state-of-the-art data-efficient reinforcement learning agent, by 18-to-7 in the Atari 100k benchmark, despite EfficientZero having the same training budget and 1.8 times the planning budget, and Olive using no policy learning whatsoever. The source code is available at github.com/ibm/atari-active-learning.

Most industrial recommender systems use collaborative filtering (CF) to offer personalized recommendations. However, CF inherently compromises user privacy, as it requires users to share preferences to receive accurate suggestions. Previous privacy-preserving methods for CF have offered some concealment from centralized systems but often sacrifice privacy, scalability, and accuracy, and remain vulnerable to malicious attacks.

We introduce a novel Selective Privacy Preserving (SP2) paradigm that empowers users to define their privacy by labeling personal ratings as public (shareable) or private (stored only on the user's device). The SP2 framework operates in two stages: (i) an initial recommendation model is built from all publicly shared ratings, and (ii) this public model is then refined on each user's device using their private ratings.

We thoroughly analyze the relationship between out-of-sample performance and Bayesian evidence (marginal likelihood) in Bayesian neural networks (BNNs), alongside assessing the performance of BNN ensembles, all using the Boston housing dataset. Employing state-of-the-art nested sampling, we numerically sample the complete (non-Gaussian and multimodal) network posterior to estimate Bayesian evidence. We examine network models with up to 156 trainable parameters, featuring zero to four hidden layers, $\tanh$ or ReLU activation functions, and with or without hierarchical priors. BNN ensembles are formed by deriving the posterior distribution over networks, re-weighting individual BNN posterior samples by their Bayesian evidence. We observe a strong correlation between out-of-sample performance and evidence. Additionally, there's a notable symmetry between evidence versus model size and out-of-sample performance versus model size. ReLU activation functions consistently yield higher evidence than $\tanh$ functions, which aligns with their superior out-of-sample performance. Ensembling across architectures further enhances performance compared to individual BNNs.

Real-world prediction tasks often necessitate modeling multi-order feature interactions within user event sequences to enhance detection performance. However, current popular solutions typically encounter two limitations: they either prioritize feature interactions while neglecting sequential influence, or they focus solely on sequential information, thereby overlooking internal feature relationships within individual events and hindering effective event representation.

This paper proposes a two-level framework to capture hierarchical information within user event sequences. This involves, first, learning effective event representations based on feature interactions, and second, modeling the sequential representation of a user's historical events. Our model demonstrates significantly improved performance over state-of-the-art baselines, as evidenced by experimental results on both industrial and public datasets.

This paper investigates various time series modeling approaches. We describe forecasting methods, including linear models, ARIMA, and XGBoost, and present results from different model combinations. For probabilistic modeling, we explore approaches utilizing copulas and Bayesian inference.

Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning (PPML) focuses on safeguarding data privacy and security throughout the machine learning model development process. This field incorporates techniques like Secure Multi-Party Computation, Differential Privacy, and Homomorphic Encryption (HE), which can be integrated with various machine learning and deep learning models to protect both data privacy and user identity. This paper introduces a novel fully homomorphic encrypted wavelet neural network designed to maintain model efficiency while ensuring privacy. We evaluated its effectiveness across seven datasets from finance and healthcare, demonstrating that our proposed model achieves performance comparable to its unencrypted counterpart.

Existing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) typically rely on message passing and aggregation to learn node embeddings, a framework that inherently struggles to capture the relative positional information between nodes. To address this limitation, some GNNs introduce "anchors" – specific nodes used to infer relative positions based on their distances to other nodes. However, current anchor selection methods often choose anchors arbitrarily, which can compromise both positional awareness and feature extraction capabilities.

We argue that effective positional awareness necessitates anchors that are both evenly distributed and asymmetric. While we demonstrate that selecting anchors capable of aggregating embeddings from all nodes within a graph is an NP-hard problem, making deterministic optimal approaches impractical, we propose Position-Sensing Graph Neural Networks (PSGNNs). PSGNNs learn to select anchors through a back-propagatable process, effectively bypassing the NP-completeness challenge while ensuring robust positional awareness.

Our experiments show that PSGNNs significantly outperform state-of-the-art GNNs on various synthetic and real-world graph datasets, demonstrating substantial performance improvements and stable scalability. Specifically, PSGNNs boost AUC by over 14% for pairwise node classification and 18% for link prediction compared to existing position-aware methods. Our source code is publicly available.

We address the challenge of certifying individual fairness (IF) in feed-forward neural networks (NNs). Our focus is the $\epsilon$-$\delta$-IF framework, which, for a given NN and a data-derived similarity metric, postulates that the output difference between any two $\epsilon$-similar individuals must not exceed a predefined decision tolerance $\delta \geq 0$.

Employing various metrics, including the Mahalanobis distance, we introduce a method to approximate the resulting optimization problem. This is achieved by using piecewise-linear functions to globally bound the NN's non-linearities across the input space, providing both lower and upper bounds. We formulate this computation as a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming problem.

We demonstrate our method's ability to compute IF guarantees on four widely used fairness benchmarking datasets. Furthermore, we illustrate how this formulation can be integrated into the training process by modifying the NN loss function to promote model fairness. Our empirical results show that this approach yields NNs that are significantly fairer compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success in diverse computer vision applications. However, their use in tasks involving high-dimensional input and output, such as high-resolution image and video segmentation or 3D medical imaging, faces limitations. A primary constraint arises during training: storing network activations for backpropagation often demands memory exceeding current hardware capabilities, particularly for 3D problems.

Inspired by signal propagation in physical networks, governed by the hyperbolic Telegraph equation, we propose a fully conservative hyperbolic network designed for high-dimensional input and output. We introduce a coarsening operation that enables completely reversible CNNs. This is achieved by employing a learnable Discrete Wavelet Transform and its inverse to coarsen and interpolate the network state, while also adjusting the number of channels. We demonstrate that these fully reversible networks achieve state-of-the-art comparable results in 4D time-lapse hyperspectral image segmentation and full 3D video segmentation, but with significantly reduced memory consumption that remains constant regardless of network depth. Additionally, we extend the application of these networks to...

Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are susceptible to adversarial attacks. While adding adversarial noise to training data—a technique known as standard adversarial training (SAT)—can enhance their robustness, improperly introduced noise may degrade model performance, creating an accuracy-robustness trade-off. This issue has been extensively researched in whole-image classification but remains largely unexplored in medical image analysis tasks such as segmentation, landmark detection, and object detection.

We demonstrate that for these medical imaging tasks, SAT suffers from a significant limitation: it applies a uniform level of noise across all training samples for robust DNN training. A high noise level can severely impact model performance, whereas a low noise level may not sufficiently improve robustness.

To address this, we propose an adaptive-margin adversarial training (AMAT) method. Unlike existing classification-focused adversarial training approaches, AMAT generates sample-specific adaptive adversarial noise for robust DNN training by employing a loss-defined-margin strategy.

Deep neural networks in medicine often suffer from a scarcity of large training datasets and benchmarks. While manual labeling is costly, computer simulations offer a way to generate extensive, fully labeled datasets with minimal human effort. However, models trained on simulated data typically struggle to perform well in real-world scenarios.

To overcome this "domain gap" between simulated and real laparoscopic images, we leverage recent breakthroughs in unpaired image-to-image translation. We've adapted an image-to-image translation technique to create a wide variety of realistic synthetic images from simple laparoscopic simulations. By ensuring that image content is preserved during translation, the original labels from the simulated images remain accurate for their realistic counterparts.

This approach allows us to produce a large, fully labeled synthetic dataset of realistic laparoscopic images. We demonstrate that this dataset can effectively train models for liver segmentation in laparoscopic images, achieving average Dice scores up to 0.89 in some patients without any manual labeling of laparoscopic images.

Fair machine learning research often, and perhaps simplistically, assumes a single decision-maker and a stable population. Yet, the real-world scenarios that necessitate this research frequently involve competitive markets with multiple decision-makers. In such contexts, it's more realistic to expect only a portion of these decision-makers to adopt non-mandatory fairness policies—a phenomenon political philosophers term "partial compliance."

This raises critical questions: How does the strategic behavior of individuals in a partially compliant system influence outcome allocation? If, for instance, k% of employers voluntarily implement a fairness initiative, should we anticipate a proportional k% improvement in overall outcomes compared to universal adoption? Or will the complexities of partial compliance dilute the intended benefits? Furthermore, how do the conclusions of an auditor change when adopting a global perspective versus a local one?

To explore these questions, we introduce a straightforward model of an employment market and employ simulation to analyze the impact of both interaction and incentive effects on outcomes and auditing metrics. Our primary findings indicate that, at equilibrium:

1.  Partial compliance (involving k% of employers) often yields significantly less than k% progress toward the outcomes achievable with full compliance.
2.  This discrepancy is exacerbated when fair employers prioritize global matching.

This paper demonstrates that metric learning faces a significant "inseparable problem" without informative sample mining. Given that inseparable samples often overlap with hard samples, existing informative sample mining strategies designed to address this issue can introduce drawbacks like objective function instability. To mitigate this, we introduce Adaptive Neighborhood Metric Learning (ANML), a novel distance metric learning algorithm. ANML employs two adaptive thresholds to identify inseparable similar and dissimilar samples during training, integrating sample removal and metric parameter learning within a single process. Due to ANML's inherent non-continuity, we developed the "log-exp mean function" to create a continuous surrogate, enabling efficient optimization via gradient descent. Like Triplet loss, ANML can learn both linear and deep embeddings. Our analysis reveals interesting properties; for instance, when learning linear embeddings, ANML encompasses well-known metric learning algorithms such as Large Margin Nearest Neighbor (LMNN) and Neighborhood Components Analysis (NCA) as special cases.

Explainable AI (XAI) is crucial for understanding black-box machine learning, especially in fields demanding high reliability and transparency, such as medical diagnostics or applications subject to GDPR's transparency requirements. These contexts necessitate auditing the reasoning behind a classifier's decisions. While visualizations are commonly used for explanations, they often lack the expressiveness to differentiate subtle visual variations (e.g., open vs. closed eyes) or accurately convey the impact of missing features and inter-feature relationships.

More expressive symbolic surrogate models offer an alternative, but they typically require symbolic inputs not readily available in most computer vision tasks. This paper addresses this challenge by leveraging the inherent features learned by a feed-forward convolutional deep neural network (DNN) to construct comprehensive, verbal explanations of its decision-making process. We extract the semantic meaning of these features through a concept analysis method, trained on human-understandable visual concepts. An Inductive Logic Programming (ILP) method then generates the final explanation.

This paper investigates vehicle re-identification by comparing image distances within CNN latent spaces. We first evaluate the effectiveness of various distance metrics—minimal Euclidean distance (MED), minimal cosine distance (MCD), and residue of sparse coding reconstruction (RSCR)—using features extracted from five CNN architectures: ResNet18, AlexNet, VGG16, InceptionV3, and DenseNet201. These CNNs are fine-tuned and tested on the VeRi vehicle re-identification dataset. Our findings consistently show that MCD outperforms the commonly used MED, regardless of the CNN architecture, a result further corroborated on other vehicle retrieval datasets.

Secondly, we extend the traditional image-to-track process (I2TP) to a track-to-track process (T2TP) by adapting the three distance metrics for track-level comparisons. We demonstrate that T2TP surpasses I2TP in performance when using MCD and RSCR. Specifically, T2TP, particularly when combined with DenseNet201 and MCD-based metrics, achieves state-of-the-art results, outperforming existing I2TP-based models.

In summary, our experiments underscore two key insights: i) the crucial role of metric selection in vehicle re-identification, and ii) the significant performance improvement offered by T2TP over I2TP, especially when paired with MCD-based metrics.

Hardware-aware Differentiable Neural Architecture Search (DNAS) faces a significant hurdle: accurately calculating hardware metric gradients for architecture optimization. Current methods, limited by linear approximations, struggle to support custom hardware accelerators.

To address this, we introduce End-to-end Hardware-aware DNAS (EH-DNAS). This framework seamlessly integrates end-to-end hardware benchmarking with automated DNAS, enabling the creation of hardware-efficient deep neural networks across diverse platforms such as Edge GPUs, Edge TPUs, Mobile CPUs, and custom accelerators.

For a given hardware platform, EH-DNAS learns a differentiable model that predicts the end-to-end hardware performance of neural network architectures, which is then used for DNAS. We also present E2E-Perf, a specialized end-to-end hardware benchmarking tool designed for custom accelerators.

Experimental results on CIFAR10 and ImageNet demonstrate that EH-DNAS significantly boosts hardware performance, achieving an average improvement of 1.4x on custom accelerators and 1.6x on existing processors, all while preserving classification accuracy.

This paper introduces a novel approach to distributed linear filtering and prediction. We consider a random dynamical system observed by a sparse multi-agent sensor network. Drawing inspiration from consensus+innovations distributed estimation, we propose a new algorithm that merges consensus and innovations principles. The algorithm relies on a new definition of distributed observability, a weaker condition than combined global observability and network connectivity. We derive optimal gain matrices to minimize the mean-squared estimation error at each agent, and present a distributed algebraic Riccati equation for gain computation.

This paper surveys existing deep-learning approaches for analyzing complex, discrete, and irregularly patterned sequential datasets, such as financial data characterized by sudden, event-driven changes. Traditional deep-learning methods often struggle with or fail to analyze these types of datasets effectively. A systematic literature review indicates that recurrent neural network-based frameworks are predominantly employed. Performance evaluations of these deep-learning frameworks primarily rely on mean absolute error and root mean square error accuracy metrics. Identified challenges include a lack of performance robustness, methodological non-transparency, and issues concerning internal and external architectural design and configuration. Addressing these challenges presents an opportunity to significantly enhance deep-learning frameworks for complex, irregularly patterned sequential datasets.

Recent research highlights positive theoretical results for training over-parameterized neural networks, where the network's size exceeds what's necessary for low error. The core idea is that with sufficient over-parameterization, gradient-based methods implicitly keep certain network components relatively static. This means the optimization process acts as if these components are fixed at their initial random values. Explicitly fixing these components leads to the familiar random feature learning approach. Essentially, these techniques suggest that successful neural network learning is possible whenever random features can be learned successfully.

This paper begins by reviewing these techniques, offering a straightforward, self-contained analysis for one-hidden-layer networks. However, we contend that despite impressive positive outcomes, random feature approaches inherently limit what they can elucidate. Specifically, we rigorously demonstrate that random features cannot learn even a single ReLU neuron with standard Gaussian inputs unless the network size (or weight magnitude) is exponentially large. Given that a single neuron is learnable with gradient-based methods, we conclude that a comprehensive, general explanation for empirical observations remains elusive.

Word embeddings are a cornerstone of deep learning models in natural language processing. Various types of these vector representations exist, such as word2vec and GloVe. Trained on massive text corpora, embeddings learn contextual word usage, thereby capturing semantic relationships. However, the semantics captured are at the individual word level (word types) and can be ambiguous, particularly when a word type has multiple grammatical roles (e.g., noun or verb). For tasks like question answering, part-of-speech and named entity information are crucial, yet incorporating these attributes into neural models typically increases input dimensionality. This research proposes using holographic compression to represent a token, its part-of-speech, and its named entity type within the same dimensional space as a token alone. Implemented within a modified recurrent deep learning network for question answering, this approach demonstrates preserved semantic relationships and robust performance.

The increasing use of sensitive user data to train machine learning models has raised significant privacy concerns. Federated learning offers a popular privacy-preserving solution by exchanging local gradient information instead of raw data. To further strengthen privacy, local differential privacy (LDP) can be integrated into federated learning. However, existing LDP-based federated learning approaches face three key challenges: 1) noisy data often remains too close to its original value, risking information leakage; 2) they introduce substantial variance to estimated averages, leading to poor accuracy; and 3) the privacy budget can explode due to the high dimensionality of deep learning model weights.

This paper proposes a novel LDP mechanism for federated learning designed to overcome these limitations. Our mechanism ensures that privatized data is distinctly different from its original form while introducing less variance. Furthermore, it mitigates the curse of dimensionality by strategically splitting and shuffling model updates. Empirical evaluations using MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate that our solution not only achieves superior deep learning performance but also provides a robust privacy guarantee.

Deep learning algorithms have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in Computer Vision. In recent years, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have been successfully applied to image generation, finding widespread use in photo editing, image design, computer animation, real-time rendering for large-scale scenes, and visual effects in movies. However, during texture synthesis, current state-of-the-art CNNs struggle to preserve the spatial location of textures within an image, often leading to significant distortion. To address this, we propose a novel image generation approach that incorporates a semantic segmentation pre-processing step using deep learning algorithms, and we analyze the resulting outcome.

This paper outlines the baseline approach for the 2nd Covid-19 Competition, held as part of the AIMIA Workshop at ECCV 2022. We introduce the COV19-CT-DB database, which contains approximately 7,700 3-D CT scans annotated for COVID-19 detection. A subset of this database, specifically COVID-19 cases, includes further annotations for four distinct severity levels. We have divided the database, and particularly its COVID-19 subset, into training, validation, and test datasets. The training and validation sets are designated for developing and refining machine learning models, while the test set will be used for final model evaluation. Our baseline approach employs a deep learning architecture, specifically a CNN-RNN network, and its performance on the COVID19-CT-DB database is reported.

Optimal Transport (OT) is a powerful tool in machine learning, but its high computational cost often limits its practical application. To overcome this, we introduce SPOT (Scalable Push-forward of Optimal Transport), an implicit generative learning framework. SPOT reframes the optimal transport problem as a minimax problem by approximating the optimal transport plan as a pushforward of a reference distribution. This allows us to efficiently solve OT problems using primal-dual stochastic gradient algorithms. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the density of the optimal transport plan can be reconstructed using neural ordinary differential equations. Our experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that SPOT is robust, converges well, and enables efficient sampling from the optimal transport plan, which is beneficial for tasks like domain adaptation.

Machine learning models often operate in conjunction with human experts, particularly when the model's confidence in its predictions is low, allowing it to defer to human judgment. Our objective is to develop methods that guarantee both accuracy and fairness within these hybrid prediction systems, which integrate machine learning inferences with human expert input.

Previous research on "deferral systems" in classification typically addresses scenarios involving a single expert. This work has concentrated on simultaneously training an inference model and a deferral system, while accounting for the expert's inaccuracies and biases.

Our research expands this concept to situations where multiple experts are accessible, each possessing distinct areas of expertise and potential biases. We introduce a framework that concurrently learns a classifier and a deferral system. This deferral system strategically routes low-confidence predictions to one or more human experts.

We validated our framework using both a synthetic dataset and a content moderation dataset featuring simulated biased experts. Our findings indicate a substantial improvement in the accuracy and fairness of final predictions compared to baseline methods. Additionally, we gathered crowdsourced labels to support our evaluation.

This paper proposes OSM (One-Sided Margin), a novel loss function designed to effectively address maximum-margin classification problems. Unlike hinge loss, OSM explicitly defines the margin using hyperparameters, which then guides the classification process. Our experimental results demonstrate that OSM loss significantly accelerates training and improves accuracy compared to binary and categorical cross-entropy across various deep models for classification and optical character recognition. OSM consistently outperforms cross-entropy and hinge losses in classification accuracy for neural networks ranging from small to large architectures, while also leading to a more efficient training procedure. We achieved state-of-the-art accuracies for small networks on several benchmark datasets, including CIFAR10 (98.82%), CIFAR100 (91.56%), Flowers (98.04%), and Stanford Cars (93.91%), showcasing substantial improvements over other loss functions. Furthermore, OSM maintains superior accuracies over cross-entropy and hinge loss even for large networks. Consequently, we advocate for OSM as a compelling alternative to hinge and cross-entropy losses for training deep neural networks on classification tasks.

Biclustering, applied to a dataset, seeks to simultaneously partition both the data samples and their defining features into biclusters. Consistent biclusterings are particularly valuable for supervised classification, enabling accurate sample classification based on known feature classifications, and vice-versa. The challenge of identifying such consistent biclusterings can be reframed as a feature selection task. This involves removing irrelevant features while maximizing the total number of features to retain information. This feature selection problem can be expressed as a linear fractional 0-1 optimization problem. We propose rephrasing this as a bilevel optimization problem and introduce a heuristic algorithm for its efficient solution. Computational results demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms previous heuristic approaches in finding superior solutions.

This work introduces a **Discourse-Aware Semantic Self-Attention** encoder, which leverages linguistic annotations to process long narrative texts for reading comprehension. We extract discourse unit relations, event arguments, and coreferring mentions using existing annotation tools. Our evaluation demonstrates that these structures—particularly intra-sentential and cross-sentential discourse relations, sentence-internal semantic role relations, and long-distance coreference relations—improve overall performance. We show that assigning dedicated self-attention heads to intra-sentential and neighboring-sentence relations helps in identifying answers within extended contexts. These findings suggest that discourse-semantic annotations can enhance the generalization capabilities of self-attention models for reading comprehension.

Forecasting particulate matter (PM) concentrations in South Korea is critical due to their severe negative impact on human health. While most statistical and machine learning methods assume independent and identically distributed data (e.g., Gaussian distribution), time series data like air pollution and weather patterns violate this assumption. This study employs the maximum correntropy criterion for regression (MCCR) loss to analyze the statistical properties of air pollution and weather data. We rigorously adjusted for the complex and heavily-tailed seasonality of this data, even after deseasonalization. The MCCR loss was then applied to various models, including traditional statistical and advanced machine learning models. Our findings indicate that MCCR loss is more suitable than the conventional mean squared error loss for predicting extreme values.

Support Vector Machines (SVMs) are powerful machine learning models known for their high accuracy across diverse classification tasks, making them a popular choice for various embedded applications. However, embedding SVM classifiers presents a challenge due to their computationally intensive nature. This inherent complexity drives the need for hardware implementations of SVMs to achieve high-performance computing while managing costs and power consumption.

This paper focuses on developing an optimized embedded SVM classifier specifically for a low-cost, handheld device aimed at early melanoma detection in primary healthcare settings. Melanoma, the most aggressive form of skin cancer, significantly contributes to mortality rates, underscoring the importance of early diagnosis.

We propose a hardware/software co-design approach to implement the SVM classifier on an FPGA, effectively enabling melanoma detection on a chip. Our implementation, utilizing a modern hybrid FPGA (Zynq) and leveraging the UltraFast High-Level Synthesis design methodology, demonstrates efficient on-chip melanoma classification. The hardware implementation achieved a classification accuracy of 97.9% and a remarkable hardware acceleration rate of 21. This was accomplished with minimal resource utilization (only 3%) and low power consumption (1.69W). These results confirm that our system-on-chip meets critical embedded system requirements, delivering high performance with low resource utilization, power consumption, and cost, all while ensuring efficient operation.

Many human-interactive AI systems define "identity" using a static, discrete set of attributes—a stark contrast to critical theory's view of identity as fluid, interactively constructed, and performative. We translate these critical insights for machine learning, proposing identity as "autopoietic": a continuous process of formation and function. We argue that the prevailing AI paradigm for identity rigidifies existing categories and power imbalances because it lacks iterative feedback to models. This critique extends to current AI fairness practices, which often perpetuate the default paradigm. We then apply our autopoietic theory to outline approaches for multilevel optimization and relational learning. Though open questions remain, we envision AI capable of expressing human identity as a perpetually evolving relationship.

Estimating high-order conditional independence (CI) relationships among random variables poses a significant challenge when learning causal models from data. However, low-order CI tests are reliably performed even with limited observations, suggesting an alternative approach: inferring causal structures primarily from these more accessible low-order CIs. Recent studies have demonstrated that, particularly for sparse true causal models, structures derived from zero- and first-order conditional independencies can closely approximate the underlying models. The critical hurdle then becomes developing methods that accurately account for a given set of low-order CIs.

This paper introduces an algorithm designed to compute a faithful graphical representation from a given set of conditional independencies, specifically those of order less than or equal to a small fixed number, $k$. This work extends and refines previous research on learning from pairwise marginal independencies.
